description: Select the correct switching converter topology by analyzing input/output voltage ratio, power level, isolation requirements, and component stress. Covers buck, boost, buck-boost, SEPIC, Cuk, flyback, forward, half-bridge, and full-bridge with duty cycle mapping, CCM/DCM boundaries, and right-half-plane zero implications.

steps.description: Capture the electrical requirements that drive topology selection: input voltage range, output voltage and current, isolation needs, efficiency target, cost and size constraints.

inputs.name: input-voltage-range
inputs.desc: Minimum and maximum input voltage in volts (e.g., 36V to 72V for telecom, 85V to 265V for universal AC-DC)

inputs.name: output-voltage-current
inputs.desc: Required output voltage and maximum load current, plus any regulation accuracy requirement

inputs.name: power-level-watts
inputs.desc: Total output power in watts, which is the primary topology discriminator

inputs.name: isolation-requirement
inputs.desc: Whether galvanic isolation is needed and at what voltage rating, or non-isolated is acceptable

outputs.name: duty-cycle-range
outputs.desc: Calculated duty cycle range across input voltage range for candidate topologies using D = Vout/(Vin*eta) for buck, D = 1 - (Vin*eta/Vout) for boost

outputs.name: topology-candidates
outputs.desc: Filtered list of viable topologies based on power level (buck/boost under 150W, flyback under 200W, forward under 500W, half-bridge under 1kW, full-bridge above 500W) and isolation needs

process: Calculate the voltage conversion ratio Vout/Vin at minimum and maximum input voltage. Ratios above 4:1 or below 1:4 stress single-stage topologies and may require two stages or transformer turns ratio adjustment.

For each candidate topology, compute the duty cycle at minimum and maximum Vin. Flag any topology where duty cycle exceeds 0.8 (excessive switch stress) or falls below 0.1 (current pulse issues). For boost-derived topologies, note that duty cycle above 0.5 introduces right-half-plane zero.

Calculate the CCM/DCM boundary: Lcrit = (Vout * (1-D)) / (2 * fsw * Iout_min) for buck. If the minimum load is light, determine whether DCM operation is acceptable or forced-CCM with synchronous rectification is needed.

If isolation is required, eliminate buck, boost, buck-boost, SEPIC, and Cuk (unless coupled-inductor variants are considered). Rank flyback (under 150W, multiple outputs easy), forward (under 500W, better cross-regulation), half-bridge (under 1kW, good transformer utilization), full-bridge (above 500W, best for high power).
Output the candidate list with duty cycle ranges and flag any topology operating near its stress limits.

steps.description: Calculate voltage and current stress on switches, diodes, inductors, and capacitors for each candidate topology to identify the one with lowest total component cost and loss.

inputs.name: duty-cycle-range
inputs.desc: Duty cycle range from requirements capture

inputs.name: topology-candidates
inputs.desc: List of viable topologies to analyze

outputs.name: switch-stress-table
outputs.desc: For each topology: peak voltage across switch (Vin for buck, Vout for boost, Vin+Vout*N for flyback), peak and RMS current through switch

outputs.name: passive-stress-table
outputs.desc: For each topology: inductor peak current and energy storage, output capacitor RMS ripple current, input capacitor RMS current

process: For each candidate topology, calculate switch voltage stress. Buck: Vds_max = Vin_max + spike. Boost: Vds_max = Vout + spike. Flyback: Vds_max = Vin_max + N*Vout + Vleak_spike. Forward: Vds_max = Vin_max * (1 + 1/n_reset). Half-bridge: Vds_max = Vin_max. Full-bridge: Vds_max = Vin_max. Add 20% margin for ringing.

Calculate switch RMS current. Buck: Isw_rms = Iout * sqrt(D). Boost: Isw_rms = Iout/(1-D) * sqrt(D). These determine conduction loss. Calculate peak current including ripple: Ipk = Iavg + deltaI/2 where deltaI = (Vin - Vout)*D/(L*fsw) for buck.

Calculate output capacitor ripple current. Buck: Icap_rms = deltaIL / (2*sqrt(3)). Boost: Icap_rms = Iout * sqrt(D/(1-D)). High RMS current drives capacitor selection and lifetime. Flyback output cap sees the full rectified secondary current pulse.

Calculate inductor energy storage: E = 0.5*L*Ipk^2. This drives inductor size. Compare across topologies: flyback stores all energy in the magnetizing inductance (larger core), forward only stores ripple energy (smaller inductor but needs output choke).

Build a comparison table: total semiconductor VA rating, total magnetics energy, total capacitor ripple current. The topology with the lowest aggregate stress at the target operating point is the best candidate.

steps.description: Determine the boundary between continuous and discontinuous conduction mode across the load range and decide whether to design for CCM, DCM, or mixed-mode operation.

inputs.name: switch-stress-table
inputs.desc: Switch stress for selected topology

inputs.name: passive-stress-table
inputs.desc: Passive component stress data

outputs.name: inductance-selection
outputs.desc: Selected inductance value with rationale for CCM vs DCM operation, including critical inductance calculation

outputs.name: operating-mode-map
outputs.desc: Map showing CCM/DCM regions across input voltage and load current, with transition boundary marked

process: Calculate critical inductance: Lcrit = D*(1-D)^2 * R / (2*fsw) for buck, Lcrit = D*(1-D)^2 * Vout / (2*fsw*Iout) for boost. At loads below the boundary current, the converter enters DCM.
For the selected topology, plot the CCM/DCM boundary across the full input voltage range. At low Vin (high D for buck), the boundary current is lower, meaning CCM is easier to maintain.

Decide: if the load range spans more than 10:1 and light-load efficiency matters, consider allowing DCM at light loads with a larger L to keep the boundary below 10-20% of full load. If the load is always above 50% of rated, design firmly in CCM.

For DCM operation: recalculate the transfer function. Buck in DCM: Vout/Vin = 2/(1 + sqrt(1 + 8*L*fsw/(D^2*R))). The plant becomes a first-order system with no right-half-plane zero, which simplifies compensation but duty cycle becomes load-dependent.

Select the inductance value. Standard practice: L = 1.5 to 3 times Lcrit at full load for reliable CCM. Lower L means higher ripple but faster transient response. Higher L means lower ripple but slower transient and larger physical size.

steps.description: Analyze the dynamic behavior of the selected topology, identify right-half-plane zeros for boost-derived converters, and determine the maximum achievable control bandwidth.

inputs.name: inductance-selection
inputs.desc: Selected inductance and operating mode

inputs.name: operating-mode-map
inputs.desc: CCM/DCM regions across operating range

outputs.name: plant-transfer-function
outputs.desc: Small-signal transfer function of the power stage including parasitic ESR zeros, LC double pole, and any RHP zeros

outputs.name: bandwidth-limit
outputs.desc: Maximum achievable crossover frequency considering RHP zero location, switching frequency, and required phase margin

process: Derive the small-signal model using state-space averaging. For buck (voltage mode): Gvd(s) = Vout/D * (1 + s*Rc*Co) / (1 + s*(Rc + RL)*Co + s^2*L*Co) where Rc is ESR, RL is inductor DCR. This is a second-order system with an ESR zero and LC double pole.

For boost and buck-boost in CCM, identify the RHP zero: fz_rhp = (1-D)^2 * R / (2*pi*L) for boost. The RHP zero frequency drops with increasing load (lower R) and higher duty cycle. At worst case (max D, max load), calculate fz_rhp_min.

Set maximum crossover frequency. For converters without RHP zero: fc_max = fsw/5 to fsw/10. For converters with RHP zero: fc_max = fz_rhp_min / 3 to fz_rhp_min / 5. If this limits bandwidth below acceptable transient response, consider current-mode control (which moves the RHP zero frequency higher) or switching to a different topology.

For current-mode control, the inner current loop converts the LC double pole to a single pole at the load, simplifying outer voltage loop compensation. The subharmonic oscillation at D > 0.5 requires slope compensation: Se = (Vout - Vin) * Rs / L where Rs is the current sense gain.
Document the complete small-signal model with numerical values at the worst-case operating point. This feeds directly into the control loop compensation design.

steps.description: Make the final topology decision by weighing component stress, dynamic limitations, thermal feasibility, cost, and size against requirements. Produce a topology specification document.

inputs.name: plant-transfer-function
inputs.desc: Small-signal model of candidate topology

inputs.name: bandwidth-limit
inputs.desc: Maximum control bandwidth achievable

outputs.name: selected-topology
outputs.desc: Final topology choice with complete rationale including stress, dynamics, cost, and size trade-offs

outputs.name: topology-specification
outputs.desc: Complete topology specification: schematic block diagram, key component ratings, switching frequency, expected efficiency, control mode, and critical design parameters

process: Score each remaining candidate on five axes: semiconductor cost (proportional to VA rating), magnetics size (proportional to energy storage), capacitor stress (proportional to RMS ripple current), control complexity (number of control loops, need for slope compensation), and thermal challenge (total power dissipation at worst case).

Check that the achievable bandwidth meets transient response requirements. If load steps require faster response than the RHP zero allows, either select a topology without RHP zero or move to current-mode control. If neither works, add output capacitance to slow the voltage excursion during transient.

Estimate efficiency at full load and 10% load. Switch conduction loss: Pcond = Irms^2 * Rds(on). Switch loss: Psw = 0.5 * Vds * Id * (tr + tf) * fsw. Inductor loss: core + copper. Capacitor ESR loss. If efficiency falls below target, consider lower fsw (larger magnetics but lower switching loss) or better switches (GaN, SiC).
Calculate approximate board area from component sizes. Inductor area dominates at low frequency, capacitor count dominates when high ripple current requires paralleling.
Write the topology specification with block-level schematic, all key parameters, and the numerical justification for each design decision. This is the input to detailed schematic design.

description: Design magnetic components (inductors and transformers) for switching converters using core material selection, area product sizing, winding loss analysis (skin and proximity effects via Dowell's method), core loss estimation (Steinmetz), and gap calculation. Produces a complete magnetic design ready for prototype.

steps.description: Derive the magnetic component requirements from the converter operating point: inductance, peak current, RMS current, AC flux swing, and operating frequency.

inputs.name: converter-operating-point
inputs.desc: Topology, switching frequency, duty cycle range, input/output voltages

inputs.name: inductance-and-current
inputs.desc: Required inductance value, peak current, RMS current, and AC ripple current at worst-case operating point

outputs.name: flux-swing
outputs.desc: AC flux density swing delta-B in Tesla, calculated from volt-seconds: delta-B = V*D / (N*Ae*fsw)

outputs.name: energy-storage
outputs.desc: 0.5*L*Ipk^2 in Joules for inductors, or VA rating for transformers, which drives core size selection

process: For inductors: calculate energy storage E = 0.5 * L * Ipk^2. This single number determines the minimum core size through the area product. Calculate AC ripple current as a fraction of DC bias: typically 20-40% of Idc for optimal size vs loss trade-off.

For transformers: calculate the VA rating = Vrms_pri * Irms_pri. For flyback, the transformer is really a coupled inductor storing energy, so use E = 0.5 * Lm * Ipk^2. For forward/half-bridge/full-bridge, the transformer transfers power without storing energy (except leakage).

Calculate the volt-second product: V*t = Vin * D / fsw for the primary. This determines the minimum turns * area product: N * Ae = V*t / (2 * delta_B_max). The allowable delta_B depends on core loss limits.

Set initial delta_B target: for ferrite at 100kHz, start with 100-150mT peak (200-300mT swing). For ferrite at 500kHz, reduce to 50-75mT peak. Higher flux means smaller core but higher core loss (roughly proportional to B^2.5 at fixed frequency).
Document all requirements in a table: L or Lm, Ipk, Irms, Iac_rms, fsw, V*t, target delta_B, operating temperature.

steps.description: Select core material grade and geometry using the area product method, matching material properties to operating frequency and geometry to mechanical and thermal constraints.

inputs.name: flux-swing
inputs.desc: Required AC flux density swing

inputs.name: energy-storage
inputs.desc: Energy storage or VA rating requirement

outputs.name: selected-core
outputs.desc: Core part number, material grade, geometry (EE, ETD, PQ, toroid, RM), Ae (effective area), le (effective length), Ve (volume), AL value

outputs.name: core-loss-density
outputs.desc: Specific core loss in mW/cm^3 at the operating frequency and flux swing, from the material datasheet Steinmetz parameters

process: Select material by frequency range. Below 500kHz: MnZn ferrite (3C90/3C95 for low loss, 3F3/N87 for general purpose). 500kHz to 3MHz: MnZn high-frequency grades (3F4/N49). Above 1MHz: NiZn ferrite or powdered iron for very high frequency. For inductors with large DC bias, consider powdered iron (Kool Mu, MPP) which has distributed gap and better energy density.

Calculate required area product: AP = Ae * Aw = (L * Ipk^2) / (Kw * J * delta_B * Ku). Kw is winding fill factor (0.3-0.4 for round wire, 0.5-0.7 for foil), J is current density (3-6 A/mm^2 for natural convection, 6-10 for forced air), Ku is utilization factor.

Select geometry. EE cores: cheapest, easiest to wind, good for cost-sensitive designs. ETD: round center post gives better winding fill than EE. PQ: lower profile than ETD at same AP. RM: shielded, good for EMI-sensitive designs. Toroid: lowest EMI (closed magnetic path), but hardest to wind and no practical air gap for inductors.
From the manufacturer catalog, find cores with AP >= calculated minimum. Take the next size up for margin. Record Ae, Aw, le, Ve, and AL (inductance per turn squared without gap).

Look up Steinmetz parameters for the selected material: Pv = k * f^alpha * B^beta (in mW/cm^3 with f in kHz, B in mT). Typical ferrite: alpha = 1.5-1.8, beta = 2.3-2.8. Calculate core loss at operating point: Pcore = Pv * Ve.

steps.description: Design the winding structure, calculate turns count, select wire gauge accounting for skin and proximity effects using Dowell's method, and estimate total winding loss.

inputs.name: selected-core
inputs.desc: Core geometry with Ae, Aw, window dimensions

inputs.name: core-loss-density
inputs.desc: Core loss at operating point for thermal budget allocation

outputs.name: winding-specification
outputs.desc: Number of turns per winding, wire type (solid, Litz, foil), wire gauge, layer count, winding order for transformers

outputs.name: winding-loss
outputs.desc: Total copper loss broken down into DC resistance loss and AC proximity/skin effect loss, with Rac/Rdc ratio

process: Calculate turns: N = L * Ipk / (Bmax * Ae) for inductors. For transformers: Npri = Vin * D / (fsw * delta_B * Ae), Nsec = Npri / turns_ratio. Round to nearest integer and verify flux density stays within limits.

Calculate skin depth: delta = 66.2 / sqrt(f_kHz) mm for copper at 25C. At 100kHz, delta = 0.21mm, so wire diameter should not exceed 2*delta = 0.42mm for full utilization. Use Litz wire (multiple individually insulated strands each below skin depth) for frequencies above 50kHz.

Apply Dowell's method for proximity effect. Calculate the number of layers p = N * d_wire / (h_window * Kw). The AC resistance factor: Fr = Rac/Rdc = G1(Q) + (2*(p^2 - 1)/3) * G2(Q) where Q = d_strand * sqrt(pi*f*mu0/(4*rho)) is the ratio of strand diameter to skin depth. G1 and G2 are hyperbolic functions. For p > 2 layers, proximity effect can increase AC loss 5-20x.

For transformers, interleave windings to reduce effective layer count. Full interleave (P-S-P-S) reduces p to 1 for each section, cutting proximity loss dramatically compared to non-interleaved (P-P-S-S). The trade-off is increased interwinding capacitance.

Calculate total winding loss: Pcu = Irms_dc^2 * Rdc + Irms_ac^2 * Rac. For inductors, Irms_dc is the DC bias current and Irms_ac is the ripple current. The AC component flows through Rac which includes skin and proximity. Litz wire: calculate Rac using individual strand diameter in Dowell's equation.

steps.description: Calculate the air gap length for inductors, verify inductance under DC bias, and address fringing flux effects near the gap.

inputs.name: winding-specification
inputs.desc: Turns count, wire type, layer structure

inputs.name: winding-loss
inputs.desc: Copper loss budget for thermal verification

outputs.name: gap-specification
outputs.desc: Air gap length in mm, gap placement (center leg, distributed, or spacer), fringing flux correction factor

outputs.name: verified-inductance
outputs.desc: Inductance value verified under DC bias conditions, including saturation margin and temperature effects

process: Calculate required gap length: lg = mu0 * N^2 * Ae / L - le/mu_r. For ferrite (mu_r ~ 2000+), the le/mu_r term is small and the gap dominates: lg = mu0 * N^2 * Ae / L. Typical gaps are 0.1mm to 2mm for power inductors.

Apply fringing flux correction. The effective gap area is larger than the core area due to fringing: Ae_eff = Ae * (1 + lg/sqrt(Ae) * ln(2*h_window/lg)). This reduces the required gap by the correction factor. For gaps larger than 10% of the center leg diameter, fringing is significant and reduces inductance less than the simple formula predicts.

Verify inductance under DC bias. Ferrite permeability drops with DC bias (B-H curve saturation). At the peak current, calculate B_dc = mu0 * N * Ipk / (lg + le/mu_r). If B_dc exceeds 300mT for standard ferrite, the core saturates. Either increase the gap, use a larger core, or switch to a material with higher Bsat (e.g., 3C97 at 500mT).

For distributed gap (powdered iron, Kool Mu), there is no discrete air gap. The permeability roll-off curve from the datasheet gives the effective permeability at a given H (= N*I/le). Calculate inductance at peak current using the rolled-off permeability, not the initial value. Typical Kool Mu loses 50% of its initial permeability at 80-100 Oe.

Document final gap specification: gap length, gap placement (center leg only, or split between center and outer legs for reduced fringing EMI), and spacer material. For EE cores, specify whether the gap is ground into the center post or uses a Mylar spacer between core halves.

steps.description: Verify thermal performance of the magnetic design, calculate total temperature rise, and produce a complete specification for prototype build.

inputs.name: gap-specification
inputs.desc: Gap length and placement details

inputs.name: verified-inductance
inputs.desc: Inductance at operating conditions

outputs.name: thermal-verification
outputs.desc: Estimated surface temperature rise from total power dissipation (core + copper loss), using thermal resistance model or empirical formula

outputs.name: prototype-specification
outputs.desc: Complete build specification: core P/N, wire type and gauge, turns count per winding, winding order, insulation layers, gap spacer thickness, expected L at zero and peak current, total loss budget

process: Sum total magnetic component loss: Ptotal = Pcore + Pcu. Verify the ratio: for a balanced design, Pcore should be roughly equal to Pcu (equal loss allocation minimizes total size). If one dominates, the design is suboptimal.

Estimate temperature rise. For ungapped ferrite cores, use the empirical formula: delta_T = Ptotal / (surface_area * h_conv). For natural convection, h_conv = 7-12 W/(m^2*K). Alternatively, use the core manufacturer's thermal resistance curve: Rth = 40 to 60 K/W for small cores (E25), 15-25 K/W for medium (E42), down to 5-10 K/W for large (E65).

Check that core temperature stays below the Curie temperature (typically 200-220C for MnZn ferrite) with adequate margin. Operating temperature should stay below 100-120C for standard grades. High-temperature grades (e.g., 3C97) allow operation to 150C.

For Litz wire, verify that the temperature rise does not cause strand-to-strand short circuits due to insulation breakdown. Polyurethane insulation (Grade 1): 130C. Polyester-imide (Grade 2): 155C. Polyamide-imide (Grade 3): 200C.

Compile the complete prototype specification. Include: core part number, bobbin or former, wire specification (type, AWG, number of strands for Litz), turns per winding, winding direction and order, insulation tape layers and voltage rating, gap spacer material and thickness, assembly notes (glue, banding, mounting). Record expected performance: L at 0A and at Ipk, Rdc, estimated Rac at fsw, core loss, total loss, temperature rise.

description: Design and verify control loop compensation for switching converters. Covers plant transfer function derivation via state-space averaging, compensator design (Type II/III), current mode vs voltage mode trade-offs, stability analysis, and digital implementation via bilinear transform.

steps.description: Derive the small-signal transfer function of the power stage using state-space averaging, identifying poles, zeros, and any right-half-plane zeros.

inputs.name: converter-topology
inputs.desc: Selected topology with schematic and component values (L, C, Rload, Rdc, ESR)

inputs.name: operating-point
inputs.desc: Nominal duty cycle, input voltage, output voltage, and load current at which to linearize

outputs.name: control-to-output-tf
outputs.desc: Gvd(s): transfer function from duty cycle perturbation to output voltage, with numerical pole and zero locations

outputs.name: line-to-output-tf
outputs.desc: Gvg(s): transfer function from input voltage perturbation to output voltage (audiosusceptibility), for input feedforward if needed

process: Write the state equations for each switch state (on and off). State variables are inductor current and capacitor voltage. For buck: during on-time, diL/dt = (Vin - Vout - iL*Rdc)/L; dVout/dt = (iL - Vout/R)/C.

Apply state-space averaging: weight each state equation by its duty cycle fraction. Introduce small-signal perturbations: d = D + d_hat, vin = Vin + v_hat_in, vout = Vout + v_hat_out, iL = IL + i_hat_L. Collect first-order AC terms, discard DC and second-order.

Solve for Gvd(s) = v_hat_out / d_hat. For voltage-mode buck: Gvd(s) = Vin * (1 + s*Rc*C) / (1 + s*(L/R + C*(Rc+Rdc)) + s^2*L*C*(1+Rc/R)). The ESR zero is at fz = 1/(2*pi*Rc*C). The LC double pole is at fp = 1/(2*pi*sqrt(L*C)).

For boost in CCM, derive the RHP zero: Gvd(s) has a zero at s = R*(1-D)^2/L (positive, meaning RHP). This limits control bandwidth to about 1/3 to 1/5 of fz_rhp. At worst case (max D, max load), calculate the minimum RHP zero frequency.

Plot the Bode diagram of Gvd(s) with numerical values. Identify the gain at DC (Vout/D for buck), the LC resonance peak (Q = R*sqrt(C/L) for lightly damped), the ESR zero, and the -2 slope (-40 dB/decade) from the double pole. This is the plant that the compensator must shape.

steps.description: Choose between voltage mode control, peak current mode control, and average current mode control based on plant characteristics, transient requirements, and topology constraints.

inputs.name: control-to-output-tf
inputs.desc: Plant transfer function with pole/zero locations

inputs.name: line-to-output-tf
inputs.desc: Audiosusceptibility for feedforward assessment

outputs.name: selected-control-mode
outputs.desc: Chosen control mode with rationale: VMC for simplicity when no RHP zero, PCM for fast line rejection and single-pole plant, ACM for PFC or high-current applications

outputs.name: modified-plant-tf
outputs.desc: Effective plant transfer function seen by the outer voltage loop after inner current loop closure (for current mode), or same as input for voltage mode

process: Evaluate voltage mode control (VMC). Advantages: simple, single feedback loop, no current sensor needed. Disadvantages: LC double pole requires Type III compensation, poor inherent line rejection. Best for: buck converters where bandwidth is not critical, or when digital control provides computational compensation.

Evaluate peak current mode control (PCM). The inner current loop forces inductor current to follow the control voltage, converting the LC double pole to a single pole at fload = 1/(2*pi*R*C). This simplifies compensation to Type II. PCM provides cycle-by-cycle overcurrent protection. Disadvantage: subharmonic oscillation at D > 0.5 requires slope compensation with Se >= Sf/2 where Sf = (Vout - Vin)*Rs/L (for buck).

Evaluate average current mode control (ACM). The inner loop regulates average (not peak) inductor current, eliminating the peak-to-average error. Required for PFC (power factor correction) where the current reference is a rectified sine. Also used for paralleled converters for current sharing. More complex: requires a current error amplifier with its own compensation.

For boost-derived topologies with RHP zero: PCM is strongly preferred because the modified plant sees the RHP zero at a higher frequency (due to the current loop pushing it), allowing wider bandwidth. For buck: VMC with Type III is adequate for most applications unless fast transient response (less than 10 switching cycles) is required.

Select the control mode and document the modified plant transfer function. For PCM, the voltage loop sees: Gvc(s) = Ri / (Rs * (1 + s/w_p)) where w_p = 1/(R*C) and Ri is the control-to-inductor-current gain.

steps.description: Design the feedback compensator (Type I, II, or III) to achieve target crossover frequency with adequate phase and gain margins. Produce component values for the error amplifier network.

inputs.name: selected-control-mode
inputs.desc: VMC, PCM, or ACM with rationale

inputs.name: modified-plant-tf
inputs.desc: Plant transfer function as seen by the compensator

outputs.name: compensator-transfer-function
outputs.desc: Gc(s) with pole and zero locations, gain at crossover, and component values (R1, R2, R3, C1, C2, C3 for Type III around an op-amp or error amplifier)

outputs.name: loop-gain-analysis
outputs.desc: T(s) = Gc(s) * Gvd(s) * H(s) plotted: crossover frequency, phase margin (target >45 deg), gain margin (target >10 dB), and conditional stability check

process: Set the target crossover frequency fc. For converters without RHP zero: fc = fsw/10 to fsw/5. For converters with RHP zero: fc = fz_rhp / (3 to 5). Higher fc gives faster transient response but more noise sensitivity.

Choose compensator type. Type I (integrator): single pole at origin, provides infinite DC gain, zero steady-state error. Adequate only if plant has no resonant peak (e.g., PCM buck at light load). Type II (integrator + one zero + one pole): places zero below crossover to boost phase, pole above crossover for noise rejection. Adequate for single-pole plants (PCM). Type III (integrator + two zeros + two poles): places two zeros to compensate for the LC double-pole phase lag. Required for VMC with LC plant.

Place zeros and poles. Type III for VMC buck: place both zeros at or slightly below the LC resonance fp to cancel the -180 degree phase shift. Place both high-frequency poles at or above the ESR zero frequency and half the switching frequency (whichever is lower). Set the mid-band gain to make |T(jw)| cross 0 dB at fc.

Calculate component values. For a Type III compensator using an op-amp: R1 sets the DC gain, C1 and R2 set the lower zero and integrator pole, C2 and R3 set the upper zero, C3 sets the upper high-frequency pole. Formulas: fz1 = 1/(2*pi*R2*C1), fz2 = 1/(2*pi*(R1+R3)*C3), fp1 = 1/(2*pi*R2*C1*C2/(C1+C2)), fp2 = 1/(2*pi*R3*C3).

Verify with complete loop gain Bode plot. Check: phase margin > 45 degrees (60 preferred), gain margin > 10 dB, no conditional stability (gain does not re-cross 0 dB at lower frequencies), sufficient gain at line frequency for input rejection.

steps.description: Verify loop stability across all operating conditions (input voltage range, load range, temperature) using Bode plots, step responses, and Nyquist criteria for edge cases.

inputs.name: compensator-transfer-function
inputs.desc: Designed compensator with component values

inputs.name: loop-gain-analysis
inputs.desc: Nominal loop gain Bode plot

outputs.name: stability-across-conditions
outputs.desc: Phase and gain margin at each corner of the operating range (min/max Vin, min/max load), with worst-case condition identified

outputs.name: transient-response-prediction
outputs.desc: Predicted output voltage deviation for specified load step, calculated from loop gain bandwidth and output capacitance

process: Recalculate the plant transfer function at all four corners: (Vin_min, Iout_min), (Vin_min, Iout_max), (Vin_max, Iout_min), (Vin_max, Iout_max). The plant changes significantly: DC gain varies with Vin (buck) or D (boost), resonance frequency shifts with load, and damping changes.

Plot loop gain T(s) at each corner with the fixed compensator. The compensator is designed at one operating point (typically worst case for phase margin) and must provide adequate stability everywhere else. Minimum phase margin across all corners must exceed 30 degrees (45 preferred).

For current-mode control, verify slope compensation adequacy across the full duty cycle range. At D > 0.5 without sufficient slope compensation, the current loop becomes unstable (subharmonic oscillation at fsw/2). Check: Se/Sf > 0.5 at maximum duty cycle.

Predict transient response. For a load step delta_I, the initial voltage deviation is delta_V = delta_I * ESR (fast, within one switching cycle) plus delta_V_cap = delta_I / (C * 2*pi*fc) (slow, limited by bandwidth). Total peak deviation = ESR step + bandwidth-limited droop. Verify this meets the output voltage tolerance.

Document the worst-case operating point for phase margin, the transient response prediction, and any conditional stability risks. If any corner fails, iterate on the compensator design: adjust zero/pole placement or reduce crossover frequency.

steps.description: Convert the analog compensator to a digital implementation using bilinear transform (Tustin's method), verify discrete-time stability, and address practical digital control issues.

inputs.name: stability-across-conditions
inputs.desc: Verified stability margins at all operating corners

inputs.name: transient-response-prediction
inputs.desc: Expected dynamic performance

outputs.name: digital-compensator-coefficients
outputs.desc: Difference equation coefficients (b0, b1, b2, a1, a2) for direct implementation in firmware, with fixed-point scaling factors if applicable

outputs.name: digital-implementation-spec
outputs.desc: ADC sampling rate, PWM resolution, computational delay budget, anti-aliasing filter requirements, and fixed-point word length analysis

process: Apply the bilinear transform: substitute s = (2/Ts) * (z-1)/(z+1) into the continuous compensator Gc(s). This maps the left-half s-plane into the unit circle z-plane, preserving stability. Pre-warp the critical frequencies: w_prewarp = (2/Ts) * tan(w_analog * Ts/2) to correct frequency warping at crossover.

Convert the z-domain transfer function Gc(z) to a difference equation: y[n] = b0*x[n] + b1*x[n-1] + b2*x[n-2] - a1*y[n-1] - a2*y[n-2]. These coefficients go directly into firmware. Normalize so a0 = 1.

Account for computational delay. One sample period of delay (from ADC conversion + computation + PWM update) adds phase lag: phi_delay = -360 * fc * Ts degrees. At fc = fsw/10 and Ts = 1/fsw, this is -36 degrees. Reduce crossover frequency or use predictive methods if the delay eats too much phase margin.

For fixed-point implementation, determine the required word length. The coefficients must be represented with enough precision that the realized pole/zero locations do not shift excessively. Rule of thumb: 16-bit coefficients are adequate for crossover up to fsw/10; higher ratios or very underdamped plants may need 32-bit.

Specify ADC requirements: sampling rate (at least 2x switching frequency, preferably synchronized to PWM), resolution (10-12 bits is typical; each LSB represents Vout_range/2^N), and anti-aliasing filter (RC low-pass with corner at fsw/2 or the Nyquist frequency of the ADC). Document the complete digital control specification ready for firmware development.

description: Design gate driver circuits for power MOSFETs and IGBTs covering gate charge analysis, driver current sizing, bootstrap circuits, dead time calculation, Miller effect mitigation, isolated driver selection, and layout for minimal gate loop inductance.

steps.description: Analyze gate charge requirements from the MOSFET/IGBT datasheet and size the gate driver current capability for target switching speed.

inputs.name: switch-datasheet
inputs.desc: MOSFET or IGBT datasheet with Qg (total gate charge), Qgs (gate-source charge), Qgd (gate-drain Miller charge), Vgs(th), and gate charge curve

inputs.name: switching-speed-target
inputs.desc: Target turn-on and turn-off times in nanoseconds, or maximum dv/dt and di/dt if constrained by EMI

outputs.name: driver-current-requirement
outputs.desc: Peak source and sink current in amps: Ig = Qg / t_sw for total, or Ig_miller = Qgd / t_miller for the critical Miller plateau phase

outputs.name: gate-resistor-value
outputs.desc: External gate resistor value to achieve target switching speed: Rg = (Vdr - Vplateau) / Ig_desired for turn-on, accounting for driver output impedance

process: Read the gate charge curve from the datasheet. Identify three regions: Qgs (gate voltage rises from 0 to threshold, no drain current flows), Qgd (Miller plateau where Vgs is flat and Vds falls, this determines dv/dt), and the final charge from plateau to Vgs_drive (current redistribution complete).

Calculate minimum driver current for target switching time. For the Miller plateau: Ig = Qgd / t_dv. The dv/dt during Miller plateau is approximately Vds / t_dv. For a 400V bus with 50ns dv/dt target: Ig = Qgd / 50ns. If Qgd = 20nC, then Ig = 400mA peak.

Size the gate resistor. During turn-on Miller plateau: Rg_on = (Vdriver - Vplateau) / Ig_on. Typically Vdriver = 10-12V for MOSFETs, Vplateau = 4-5V. For 400mA drive: Rg_on = 6V / 0.4A = 15 ohms. Include driver output impedance (typically 1-5 ohms).

Calculate gate driver power dissipation: Pgate = Qg * Vdriver * fsw. For Qg = 50nC, Vdriver = 12V, fsw = 100kHz: Pgate = 60mW. This is dissipated in the gate resistor and driver, split roughly equally between turn-on and turn-off paths.

For separate turn-on and turn-off resistors (Rg_on and Rg_off with diode steering): use a smaller Rg_on for faster turn-on (lower switching loss) and a smaller Rg_off for faster turn-off, but different from each other to independently optimize di/dt and dv/dt.

steps.description: Design the bootstrap power supply for high-side gate drivers in half-bridge and full-bridge topologies, including capacitor sizing, diode selection, and refresh considerations.

inputs.name: driver-current-requirement
inputs.desc: Peak gate current and total gate charge per cycle

inputs.name: gate-resistor-value
inputs.desc: Gate resistor values for switching speed control

outputs.name: bootstrap-capacitor-value
outputs.desc: Minimum bootstrap capacitor value in uF, calculated from charge balance: Cboot >= Qg / delta_Vboot where delta_Vboot is allowable droop (typically 0.5-1V)

outputs.name: bootstrap-diode-spec
outputs.desc: Bootstrap diode requirements: reverse voltage rating, forward recovery time, reverse recovery charge, and maximum forward current

process: Calculate the total charge drawn from the bootstrap capacitor per switching cycle: Qtotal = Qg + Iqbs * t_on + Qls where Iqbs is the driver quiescent current and Qls is level shifter charge. The bootstrap cap must supply this without excessive voltage droop.

Size the bootstrap capacitor: Cboot = Qtotal / delta_Vboot_max. Allow 0.5 to 1V droop. With Qtotal = 100nC and delta_V = 0.5V: Cboot = 200nF minimum. Use 10x larger (2.2uF) for margin and to handle startup charging transients. Ceramic X7R or X5R is preferred for low ESR.

Select the bootstrap diode. The diode must block Vbus when the high-side switch is on. Rating: Vr >= Vbus + margin. Forward recovery must be fast enough (< 50ns) to charge the bootstrap cap during the low-side on-time. Ultra-fast recovery or Schottky diodes for low reverse recovery charge to prevent shoot-through current during high-side turn-on.

Check refresh conditions. The bootstrap capacitor recharges only when the low-side switch is on (Vs node near ground). For high duty cycles (D > 0.95), the recharge time may be insufficient. Maximum duty cycle: D_max = 1 - (t_refresh / Tsw) where t_refresh accounts for diode forward recovery + RC charging time constant. If 100% duty cycle is needed, use a charge pump or isolated supply instead.

Calculate worst-case undervoltage lockout (UVLO) margin. At startup, the bootstrap cap starts uncharged. The IC typically has UVLO at Vboot = 8-9V. First pulse width must be limited until the bootstrap is charged. Verify that the initial low-side pulse charges the cap above UVLO before the first high-side pulse.

steps.description: Calculate dead time between complementary switches to prevent shoot-through, accounting for propagation delay mismatch, MOSFET turn-off tail, and body diode conduction losses.

inputs.name: bootstrap-capacitor-value
inputs.desc: Bootstrap capacitor and charging circuit parameters

inputs.name: bootstrap-diode-spec
inputs.desc: Bootstrap diode characteristics

outputs.name: dead-time-value
outputs.desc: Dead time in nanoseconds for both rising and falling edges, with breakdown of each contributing factor

outputs.name: body-diode-loss
outputs.desc: Power dissipated in MOSFET body diode during dead time, which determines the efficiency penalty of conservative dead time

process: Identify all propagation delay sources: driver IC internal delay (tpd_on, tpd_off from datasheet, typically 20-100ns), gate RC time constant (Rg * Ciss), and MOSFET turn-off tail (time from Vgs = Vth to Vds rises, depends on Qgd/Ig).

Calculate minimum dead time: td_min = max(tpd_on) - min(tpd_off) + t_fall_margin. Account for worst-case skew between high and low side driver propagation delays. Add temperature margin (propagation delay increases 10-20% from 25C to 125C).

Calculate body diode conduction loss during dead time. During dead time, the inductor current flows through the body diode (or external Schottky): P_dt = Vf * Iload * 2 * td * fsw. With Vf = 0.7V (Si body diode), Iload = 10A, td = 100ns, fsw = 100kHz: P_dt = 140mW. For GaN FETs with no body diode, reverse conduction is through the channel at higher voltage drop.

For adaptive dead time, the controller detects zero-voltage switching conditions and minimizes dead time dynamically. This reduces body diode losses and enables ZVS in resonant topologies. Implementation requires fast comparators to detect the Vs node voltage transition.

Set dead time value with margin: td = td_min * 1.5, rounded up to the nearest 10ns. For half-bridge drivers with integrated dead time (e.g., 100ns typical in ICs like IR2110), verify that the IC default is adequate. If not, use a driver with programmable dead time or generate non-overlapping signals externally.

steps.description: Analyze and prevent parasitic Miller turn-on caused by high dv/dt on the drain coupling through Cgd to the gate, potentially causing catastrophic shoot-through in half-bridge configurations.

inputs.name: dead-time-value
inputs.desc: Dead time settings for complementary switches

inputs.name: body-diode-loss
inputs.desc: Body diode loss during dead time

outputs.name: miller-mitigation-design
outputs.desc: Design measures to prevent Miller turn-on: gate pull-down resistance, active Miller clamp, negative gate bias, or Kelvin source connection

outputs.name: dv-dt-immunity
outputs.desc: Calculated dv/dt immunity in V/ns showing the maximum drain slew rate the gate can withstand without false turn-on

process: Calculate the Miller-induced gate voltage. When the complementary switch turns on, the drain of the off switch slews at dv/dt. The capacitive divider Cgd and Cgs couples this to the gate: Vgs_induced = dv/dt * Cgd * Rg / (1 + Cgd/Cgs). If this exceeds Vgs(th), the off device turns on and shoot-through occurs.

Calculate dv/dt immunity: (dv/dt)_max = Vgs(th) / (Rg_off * Cgd). For Vgs(th) = 3V, Rg_off = 10 ohms, Cgd = 100pF: (dv/dt)_max = 3V / (10 * 100e-12) = 3 V/ns. If the half-bridge switching speed exceeds this, false turn-on will occur.

Mitigation option 1: reduce gate pull-down impedance. Use a low-value Rg_off (1-2 ohms) or a dedicated low-impedance pull-down path with a PNP transistor or N-channel MOSFET clamping the gate to source. Some drivers have an active Miller clamp pin that shorts the gate to source when the output is low.

Mitigation option 2: apply negative gate bias. Driving the gate to -2V to -5V instead of 0V gives (Vgs(th) + |Vneg|) of immunity. Requires a negative supply rail from a charge pump or auxiliary winding. Standard approach for SiC MOSFETs which need -3 to -5V off-state gate voltage.

Mitigation option 3: Kelvin source connection. Use a separate source pin (available on power MOSFET packages with 4+ pins) for the gate return path. This eliminates the common-source inductance that adds to the gate voltage during high di/dt switching. The power source carries the load current; the Kelvin source carries only the gate current.

steps.description: Layout the gate driver circuit for minimal parasitic inductance in the gate loop and power loop, with proper ground plane management and isolation barrier placement.

inputs.name: miller-mitigation-design
inputs.desc: Miller turn-on prevention measures selected

inputs.name: dv-dt-immunity
inputs.desc: Required dv/dt immunity level

outputs.name: gate-loop-layout
outputs.desc: PCB layout guidelines: gate driver IC to MOSFET gate/source routing with inductance budget, decoupling capacitor placement, ground plane strategy

outputs.name: isolation-barrier-design
outputs.desc: For isolated drivers: creepage and clearance distances, transformer or optocoupler placement, primary-to-secondary capacitance minimization

process: Minimize gate loop area. The gate loop is: driver output pin -> Rg -> MOSFET gate pin -> MOSFET source pin -> driver ground pin -> driver bypass cap -> driver Vcc pin. Every nH of inductance in this loop slows switching and adds ringing. Target: less than 5nH total loop inductance.

Place the gate driver IC as close as possible to the MOSFET, ideally within 10mm. The gate resistor sits between them. The driver bypass capacitor (100nF ceramic, X7R) sits directly across the driver Vcc and GND pins, on the same layer, with vias to the driver pads.

Route the gate trace as a wide, short trace (not 50-ohm controlled impedance; the gate is not a transmission line at these lengths). Use a ground plane directly underneath for return current. The Kelvin source trace returns from the MOSFET source pad to the driver GND, separate from the power ground carrying load current.

For isolated gate drivers, maintain the isolation barrier clearance on the PCB. IEC 62368: basic insulation requires 5mm clearance and 8mm creepage for 400V working voltage. Place the isolation barrier as a slot in the PCB if needed. Keep the primary-to-secondary coupling capacitance below 3pF to reduce common-mode current that causes EMI.

For the power loop (drain of high-side -> Vbus cap -> source of low-side), minimize inductance with wide, parallel planes or thick traces on adjacent layers. The power loop inductance determines the voltage overshoot at turn-off: Vspike = Lloop * di/dt. With Lloop = 5nH and di/dt = 1A/ns: Vspike = 5V. Reducing loop inductance is more effective than adding snubbers.

description: Design EMC input filters for power converters to meet conducted emission limits. Covers LISN measurement interpretation, common mode and differential mode noise separation, filter topology design, component parasitic analysis, and damping to prevent oscillation.

steps.description: Measure or estimate conducted emissions from the converter using a LISN, interpret the spectrum, and separate common mode from differential mode noise to guide filter design.

inputs.name: converter-under-test
inputs.desc: Switching converter with operating parameters: topology, switching frequency, input voltage, output power

inputs.name: emission-standard
inputs.desc: Target standard and class (CISPR 32 Class B, FCC Part 15B, EN 55032) with quasi-peak and average limits in dBuV

outputs.name: emission-spectrum
outputs.desc: Measured or estimated conducted emission spectrum from 150kHz to 30MHz showing peaks at switching frequency harmonics, with quasi-peak and average values relative to limits

outputs.name: cm-dm-separation
outputs.desc: Separated common mode and differential mode noise spectra, identifying which mode dominates at each frequency range

process: Set up the LISN (Line Impedance Stabilization Network) per CISPR 16: 50uH inductance, 50 ohm impedance at measurement port, on both line and neutral. The LISN provides a defined impedance for the measurement and isolates the test setup from mains noise.

Measure on each line (L and N for single-phase, or + and - for DC) separately. The quasi-peak detector has a charge time constant of 1ms and discharge of 160ms for CISPR Band B (150kHz-30MHz), which weights repetitive narrowband interference (switching harmonics) lower than broadband noise.

Separate CM and DM noise. DM noise: Vdm = (VL - VN) / 2. CM noise: Vcm = (VL + VN) / 2. Use two matched probes and add/subtract, or use a CM/DM separating network. Typically, DM dominates at lower frequencies (150kHz-5MHz, driven by switching current ripple), CM dominates at higher frequencies (above 5MHz, driven by dv/dt and parasitic capacitance to ground).

Estimate emissions before measurement (for design phase). DM: the fundamental is approximately Idm * 50ohm where Idm = delta_IL (inductor current ripple) for buck. Harmonics roll off at -20dB/decade for trapezoidal current, -40dB/decade for sinusoidal. CM: Icm = Cparasitic * dv/dt at the switching node. With 10pF parasitic to chassis and 100V/ns: Icm = 1mA peak.

Calculate the required filter attenuation at each critical frequency: Atten_required = Emission_measured - Limit + 6dB_margin. The 6dB margin accounts for production variation. Separate the DM and CM attenuation requirements since they are addressed by different filter components.

steps.description: Design the differential mode EMC filter using LC stages, accounting for capacitor ESL, inductor parasitics, and the interaction between filter and converter input impedance.

inputs.name: emission-spectrum
inputs.desc: Emission levels requiring attenuation

inputs.name: cm-dm-separation
inputs.desc: DM noise spectrum and required DM attenuation in dB vs frequency

outputs.name: dm-filter-topology
outputs.desc: DM filter schematic: number of LC stages, component values, damping network. Each stage provides -40dB/decade attenuation above its resonance

outputs.name: dm-component-specs
outputs.desc: X-class capacitors (X2 for 250Vac, X1 for 440Vac) with ESR and ESL, DM inductors or leakage inductance of CM choke, with saturation current rating

process: Calculate the required DM filter order. One LC stage gives -40dB/decade above resonance. If 60dB attenuation is needed at the switching frequency: single stage resonance must be 3 decades below, which is impractical. Two stages give -80dB/decade. Place resonances to spread attenuation across the spectrum.

Select X-class capacitors. X2 rated for 250Vac or X1 for higher voltage. Film capacitors (polyester, polypropylene) are preferred for their low ESR and self-healing properties. Ceramic capacitors have lower ESL but no self-healing and may crack under thermal stress. Size: typically 0.1uF to 2.2uF per stage.

Account for capacitor parasitics. Above the self-resonant frequency (SRF = 1/(2*pi*sqrt(L_parasitic*C))), a capacitor becomes inductive and provides no filtering. Film cap SRF: 1-10MHz depending on size. Use multiple smaller caps in parallel to push the effective SRF higher, or add a small ceramic in parallel for high-frequency bypass.

Design the DM inductor. This can be the leakage inductance of the CM choke (typically 1-2% of CM inductance) or a separate inductor. For a dedicated DM inductor, powdered iron cores handle the DC bias current well. Size from required inductance and saturation current.

Check filter input impedance vs converter input impedance. The converter looks like a negative resistance to the input: Zin_conv = -Vout^2 / (Pin * eta). If the filter output impedance (resonance peak) exceeds |Zin_conv|, the system oscillates (Middlebrook criterion). Add damping: Rd in series with a Cd across the filter output. Rd = sqrt(Lf/Cf), Cd >= 4*Cf.

steps.description: Design the common mode EMC filter using CM chokes, Y-class capacitors (within safety leakage current limits), and ground connections to suppress common mode noise.

inputs.name: dm-filter-topology
inputs.desc: DM filter design (shared components may serve dual purpose)

inputs.name: dm-component-specs
inputs.desc: DM components already selected

outputs.name: cm-filter-topology
outputs.desc: CM filter schematic: CM choke inductance, Y-capacitor values, number of stages, and connection to safety ground

outputs.name: cm-choke-specification
outputs.desc: CM choke requirements: CM inductance, DM leakage inductance, saturation current (CM chokes do not saturate from differential load current since the fluxes cancel), impedance vs frequency curve

process: Calculate the required CM attenuation vs frequency. CM noise is typically dominated by higher frequencies (above 1MHz) where parasitic capacitances to chassis/earth couple the switching node dv/dt. Required attenuation at each harmonic of fsw.

Select the CM choke. Two windings on a single high-permeability core (nanocrystalline or MnZn ferrite). CM flux adds (both windings carry CM current in the same direction), providing high impedance to CM current. DM flux cancels (equal and opposite), so the choke does not saturate from load current. Typical CM inductance: 1mH to 30mH for 50/60Hz applications.

Select Y-class capacitors. Y1 rated for double-insulated connection to earth, Y2 for basic insulation. Safety limits: leakage current through Y-caps to earth must be below 0.5mA for Class I equipment (IEC 60950/62368) at rated voltage and frequency. At 250V/50Hz with 0.5mA limit: Cy_max = 0.5mA / (2*pi*50*250) = 6.4nF. Use 4.7nF standard value.

Verify CM choke impedance. The impedance curve from the datasheet shows a peak (typically at 1-10MHz for MnZn ferrite) and then rolloff at higher frequencies due to interwinding capacitance. If attenuation is needed above the peak frequency, add a second smaller CM choke with a higher resonance, or use a bead-on-lead approach for high-frequency CM current.

Integrate CM and DM filters. The standard pi-filter arrangement: Y-caps to ground, CM choke, X-caps, DM inductor (or use CM choke leakage), X-caps. Place the filter at the power entry point, before any other circuitry. The ground connection from Y-caps must go directly to the chassis/earth terminal, not through a long trace.

steps.description: Analyze how real component parasitics (ESR, ESL, interwinding capacitance, core loss) degrade filter performance at high frequency, and mitigate these effects.

inputs.name: cm-filter-topology
inputs.desc: CM filter design with component values

inputs.name: cm-choke-specification
inputs.desc: CM choke selection and characteristics

outputs.name: parasitic-model
outputs.desc: Complete parasitic model of each filter component showing ESR, ESL, interwinding capacitance, and frequency where each parasitic dominates

outputs.name: high-frequency-mitigation
outputs.desc: Measures to maintain filter effectiveness above 10MHz: ferrite beads, feed-through capacitors, shielded inductors, PCB layout rules

process: Model each capacitor as the series RLC: ideal C in series with ESR and ESL. The impedance minimum is at SRF. Above SRF, the capacitor is inductive. For a 1uF film cap with 10nH ESL: SRF = 1.6MHz. Above this, the capacitor impedance rises at +20dB/decade, providing no filtering.

Model the CM choke. Below resonance: impedance rises with frequency (inductive). At resonance (typically 1-5MHz): impedance peaks, determined by the loss tangent of the core. Above resonance: interwinding capacitance (5-50pF typical) provides a bypass path that shorts out the inductance. The choke becomes a capacitor and CM noise passes through.

Quantify the impact. Plot the ideal filter attenuation (based on nominal L and C values) versus the real attenuation (including parasitics). The real curve always hits a floor at high frequency where parasitics dominate. This floor must be below the emission limit.

Mitigation: add a small ceramic capacitor (100pF-1nF, C0G/NP0 for stable capacitance) in parallel with each film cap for high-frequency bypass. Add a ferrite bead in series with each line at the entry point for attenuation above 10MHz. Use feed-through capacitors at the chassis boundary for maximum high-frequency performance.

Layout rules: minimize the loop area between filter input and output. Keep CM choke away from switching node traces. Route the ground return for Y-caps directly to the chassis ground terminal. Maintain separation between filtered (clean) and unfiltered (noisy) sides of the PCB. Never route noisy traces under or near the CM choke.

steps.description: Add damping to prevent filter resonance from amplifying noise, verify the complete filter meets the emission standard with margin, and finalize the filter design.

inputs.name: parasitic-model
inputs.desc: Component parasitic models for realistic simulation

inputs.name: high-frequency-mitigation
inputs.desc: Additional high-frequency components selected

outputs.name: damped-filter-design
outputs.desc: Complete filter schematic with damping networks, all component values and ratings, thermal dissipation in damping resistors

outputs.name: compliance-prediction
outputs.desc: Predicted emission spectrum with filter installed, showing margin to limits at all critical frequencies and across the full 150kHz-30MHz band

process: Check filter Q at resonance. An undamped LC filter has a resonant peak of +20*log10(Q) dB, where Q = 1/(2*pi*f0*C*ESR) for the DM stage. If Q > 10, the filter amplifies noise at its resonance by > 20dB. This is worse than no filter at that frequency.

Add damping. Method 1: parallel damping: Rd in series with Cd across the filter capacitor. Rd = sqrt(L/C) for critical damping. Cd should be 4-10x the filter cap to not significantly change the filter corner frequency. Dissipation: Pd = Iac^2 * Rd at the resonance frequency.

Method 2: series damping (lossy inductor): use a powdered iron core inductor instead of ferrite, where the core loss provides natural damping at the resonance frequency. The loss tangent of powdered iron increases with frequency, providing frequency-dependent damping.

Verify Middlebrook stability criterion. The magnitude of the filter output impedance (including the resonance peak) must be less than the magnitude of the converter input impedance at all frequencies: |Zf_out(jw)| < |Zin_conv(jw)|. The converter input impedance for a regulated converter is Zin = -Vin^2/Pin (negative resistance). Use the damped filter impedance including the damping resistor.

Compile the complete filter BOM: all components with voltage ratings, current ratings, temperature ratings, and safety certifications (X/Y capacitor safety agency marks, CM choke UL/VDE approval). Predict final emissions with the filter using either simulation (SPICE with parasitic models) or calculation, showing 6dB margin to limits at all frequencies.

description: Design the thermal management system for power electronics using thermal resistance modeling, heat sink selection, thermal interface materials, and verification through calculation and measurement. Covers junction-to-ambient thermal paths, transient thermal impedance, and derating methodology.

steps.description: Compile the total power dissipation budget for the system by calculating losses in every component: switches, diodes, magnetics, capacitors, and resistive elements.

inputs.name: converter-design
inputs.desc: Complete converter schematic with all component values, switching frequency, and operating voltages and currents

inputs.name: operating-conditions
inputs.desc: Ambient temperature range (min/max), airflow conditions (natural convection, forced air with velocity), and altitude if applicable

outputs.name: loss-breakdown
outputs.desc: Itemized power loss for each component: MOSFET conduction and switching loss, diode conduction and recovery loss, inductor core and copper loss, capacitor ESR loss, gate driver loss, control IC quiescent loss

outputs.name: total-dissipation
outputs.desc: Total system power dissipation in watts at worst-case operating point (typically max load, max ambient, min input voltage for buck), and efficiency calculation

process: Calculate MOSFET losses. Conduction: Pcond = Irms^2 * Rds(on) at max junction temp (Rds(on) increases ~0.4%/C above 25C, roughly doubles at 150C). Switching: Psw = 0.5 * Vds * Id * (tr + tf) * fsw, where tr and tf include MOSFET transition times plus driver delay. Third quadrant (body diode): Pbd = Vf * I * t_dead * 2 * fsw.

Calculate diode losses (if discrete). Conduction: Pcond = Vf * Iavg + Rd * Irms^2 (use the linear model from the V-I curve at operating temperature). Reverse recovery: Prr = 0.5 * Qrr * Vr * fsw. Schottky diodes: no recovery loss but higher leakage at high temperature (check Ir at 150C).
Calculate magnetic losses from the magnetics design: Pcore + Pcopper as previously determined. These are often the second largest loss after switches.

Calculate capacitor losses: PESR = Irms_ripple^2 * ESR for each capacitor. For electrolytic caps, ESR is frequency-dependent and temperature-dependent (lower ESR at higher temp). For ceramic caps, ESR is very low but AC heating from dielectric loss (tan_delta) can matter at high ripple.

Sum all losses. The total should match the expected efficiency: eta = Pout / (Pout + Ploss_total). If efficiency is lower than target, identify the dominant loss mechanism and address it (lower Rds(on) switch, higher frequency with lower magnetics loss, etc.).

steps.description: Build the thermal resistance network from each heat source junction to ambient, including package thermal resistance, PCB spreading, thermal interface material, and heat sink.

inputs.name: loss-breakdown
inputs.desc: Power dissipation per component

inputs.name: total-dissipation
inputs.desc: System total dissipation and operating conditions

outputs.name: thermal-network-model
outputs.desc: Thermal resistance network diagram: Rth_jc (junction to case), Rth_cs (case to sink or board), Rth_sa (sink to ambient) for each major heat source, with parallel paths identified

outputs.name: junction-temperature-estimate
outputs.desc: Predicted junction temperature for each power component at worst-case conditions: Tj = Tamb + P * (Rth_jc + Rth_cs + Rth_sa)

process: For each power component, extract Rth_jc (junction to case) from the datasheet. MOSFET in D2PAK: Rth_jc = 1-3 C/W. TO-220: Rth_jc = 0.5-1.5 C/W. QFN exposed pad: Rth_jc = 3-10 C/W (through the exposed pad), Rth_jb = 20-40 C/W (through the board). The exposed pad path dominates.

For PCB-mounted components without heat sinks, calculate Rth_cs through the PCB. Thermal vias under the pad connect to copper planes: each via (0.3mm dia, 0.025mm plating) has Rth_via ~ 80 C/W. With 9 vias in parallel: Rth_vias = 80/9 = 9 C/W. The inner/bottom copper planes spread heat: Rth_spread depends on copper area and thickness.

For heat-sinked components, calculate Rth_cs through the thermal interface material (TIM). Rth_TIM = thickness / (k * area). Thermal grease: k = 0.8-5 W/(m*K), thickness 25-75um. Thermal pad: k = 1-6 W/(m*K), thickness 0.2-1mm. Phase-change material: k = 3-5 W/(m*K), self-thins to 25um under pressure. Always include contact resistance at both interfaces.

Calculate or look up Rth_sa for the heat sink. Natural convection: Rth_sa from vendor curves (function of surface area and orientation). Forced air: Rth_sa drops significantly with airflow velocity. At 2 m/s: roughly 50-70% of natural convection Rth. Use CFD or vendor curves for exact value.

Build the complete network. For components on a shared heat sink, their thermal resistances to the sink are in parallel on the heat sink node. The heat sink has a single Rth_sa to ambient. Sum the power into the shared sink and calculate the sink temperature: Tsink = Tamb + Ptotal_sink * Rth_sa. Each junction temperature: Tj_n = Tsink + Pn * (Rth_jc_n + Rth_cs_n).

steps.description: Select or design a heat sink based on the required thermal resistance, available space, airflow, and mounting method.

inputs.name: thermal-network-model
inputs.desc: Thermal resistance network with required Rth_sa

inputs.name: junction-temperature-estimate
inputs.desc: Target junction temperatures and current thermal gaps

outputs.name: heat-sink-specification
outputs.desc: Heat sink type (extruded, stamped, pin-fin, vapor chamber), dimensions, material (aluminum or copper), surface finish (anodized black for radiation), mounting method

outputs.name: thermal-budget-verification
outputs.desc: Recalculated junction temperatures with the selected heat sink confirming all components stay below rated Tj_max with margin

process: Calculate required Rth_sa: Rth_sa_required = (Tj_max - Tamb_max) / Ptotal - Rth_jc - Rth_cs. Include a 10-15C margin below Tj_max. For MOSFET with Tj_max = 150C, target Tj = 125C max.

For natural convection: Rth_sa approximately = 1 / (h * A_surface) where h = 7-12 W/(m^2*K) and A_surface includes all fin surfaces. A 50x50x25mm extruded aluminum heat sink with 8 fins has roughly A_surface = 200 cm^2, giving Rth_sa ~ 5-8 C/W.

For forced air: at 2 m/s airflow, h increases to 25-50 W/(m^2*K), reducing Rth_sa by 3-5x. Pin-fin heat sinks outperform extruded fins in forced air because they work with any airflow direction. At 3 m/s, a 50x50x10mm pin-fin can achieve Rth_sa ~ 2 C/W.

Consider the mounting interface. TO-220 to heat sink: use a mounting screw with torque spec (typically 4-6 in-lbs for #4 screw). Insulating washer (silicone pad or mica + thermal grease) adds 0.5-2 C/W. Direct mount (no isolation) gives lowest Rth_cs but the heat sink is at drain potential. SMD to PCB heat sink: either solder-reflow attach or use a thermal adhesive.

Verify the complete thermal budget: recalculate Tj for every component with the selected heat sink. Verify that no component exceeds its rated temperature under worst-case (maximum ambient, maximum load, minimum airflow for forced-air systems). Document the thermal margin for each component.

steps.description: Analyze thermal behavior under pulsed and transient load conditions using the transient thermal impedance Zth(t) to determine peak junction temperature during overloads and startup.

inputs.name: heat-sink-specification
inputs.desc: Selected heat sink with thermal characteristics

inputs.name: thermal-budget-verification
inputs.desc: Steady-state thermal analysis results

outputs.name: transient-thermal-model
outputs.desc: Foster or Cauer network model of Zth(t) for critical components, with time constants from datasheet Zth curves or extracted from step-response measurement

outputs.name: peak-temperature-under-transients
outputs.desc: Peak junction temperature during specified transient events: startup inrush, load step, overload duration before shutdown, and repetitive pulse

process: Extract transient thermal impedance Zth(t) from the MOSFET/IGBT datasheet. This is plotted as a family of curves for different duty cycles. The single-pulse curve gives Zth(t) for a step change in power. Read off Zth at the expected pulse duration.

Model Zth(t) as a Foster network: sum of parallel RC stages. Zth(t) = sum_i [Ri * (1 - exp(-t/tau_i))]. Typically 3-4 stages with time constants from microseconds (die) to seconds (package) to minutes (heat sink). Extract Ri and tau_i by curve fitting the datasheet Zth curve.

For repetitive pulses (PWM switching): the effective Zth depends on the duty cycle and frequency of the thermal pulsing (not the electrical switching frequency, but the load pulsing). At thermal frequencies much higher than the die time constant (~1ms), the junction sees the average power. At frequencies lower than the heat sink time constant, each pulse is nearly adiabatic.

Calculate peak Tj during overload. If the converter handles 2x rated load for 100ms before overcurrent protection trips: Tj_peak = Tamb + Psteady * Zth(inf) + Poverload * Zth(100ms). Use the transient Zth at 100ms from the datasheet. Verify Tj_peak < Tj_max.

For startup: the inrush current through MOSFETs before the output reaches regulation can be 5-10x the steady-state current. Calculate the energy deposited in the switch during the inrush pulse and the resulting temperature rise using Zth at the inrush duration. Pre-charge circuits or soft-start ramps reduce this stress.

steps.description: Apply derating rules to ensure long-term reliability, calculate mean time between failures using the Arrhenius model, and finalize the thermal design with a reliability target.

inputs.name: transient-thermal-model
inputs.desc: Transient thermal impedance models for critical components

inputs.name: peak-temperature-under-transients
inputs.desc: Worst-case junction temperatures under all operating scenarios

outputs.name: derating-table
outputs.desc: Derating factors applied to each component: voltage derating (typically 60-80% of rated), current derating per temperature curve, power derating above the knee temperature

outputs.name: reliability-prediction
outputs.desc: Estimated failure rate and MTBF for the thermal design, based on Arrhenius acceleration factor from junction temperature and activation energy for each failure mechanism

process: Apply voltage derating. Standard practice: operate at 60-80% of rated voltage for semiconductors, 50-70% for capacitors. Electrolytic capacitors: lifetime halves for every 10C above rated temperature. A 105C-rated cap at 85C has 4x the rated lifetime. At 95C, only 2x.

Apply temperature derating. Most semiconductors derate linearly above a knee temperature (typically 100C for MOSFET Rds(on) derating, 25C for absolute max power). The datasheet power derating curve shows: Pd_max = (Tj_max - Tc) / Rth_jc. Verify operation stays within the safe operating area (SOA).

Calculate reliability using Arrhenius model. The failure rate acceleration factor: AF = exp(Ea/k * (1/T_ref - 1/T_use)). Ea (activation energy) depends on the failure mechanism: 0.7 eV for electromigration, 1.0 eV for oxide breakdown, 0.3-0.5 eV for solder joint fatigue. Every 10C reduction in Tj roughly halves the failure rate for semiconductor mechanisms.

For electrolytic capacitors, apply the capacitor life model: Life = L0 * 2^((T_rated - T_actual)/10) * (V_rated/V_applied)^n where n = 1 to 3 depending on construction. This is often the reliability bottleneck. If predicted life is below the product target (e.g., 10 years at 24/7 operation), reduce the capacitor temperature by improving airflow or adding more capacitor area.

Compile the reliability report: list each critical component, its operating temperature, derating factor, and predicted failure rate. Sum the failure rates for the system MTBF. Identify the component with the highest failure rate (usually the electrolytic output capacitor or the MOSFET) and document the available margin.

description: Design voltage snubbers and clamp circuits for switching converters to suppress voltage spikes from parasitic inductance during switch turn-off. Covers RC snubbers, RCD clamps for flyback, active clamp circuits, and loss analysis.

steps.description: Identify the source and magnitude of voltage spikes in the switching circuit by analyzing parasitic inductances in the power loop and the energy stored in them at turn-off.

inputs.name: power-circuit-schematic
inputs.desc: Converter schematic showing all switches, diodes, magnetics, and the physical PCB layout or wiring that determines parasitic inductance

inputs.name: switching-waveforms
inputs.desc: Measured or estimated drain-source voltage and current waveforms showing the spike magnitude and ringing frequency

outputs.name: parasitic-inductance-map
outputs.desc: Identified parasitic inductances: transformer leakage inductance, PCB trace/plane inductance in the commutation loop, lead inductance of components, and their numerical values

outputs.name: spike-energy
outputs.desc: Energy stored in each parasitic inductance at the moment of turn-off: E = 0.5 * Lpar * Ipk^2, which must be absorbed by the snubber or clamp

process: Identify the commutation loop: the path through which current transfers from the turning-off device to the freewheeling path. For a buck converter, this is: MOSFET drain -> input capacitor -> MOSFET source -> freewheeling diode -> inductor. Every inductance in this loop contributes to the voltage spike.

Estimate parasitic inductances. PCB trace: approximately 1nH/mm for a trace over a ground plane, 5-10nH/mm for a trace without a nearby return path. Leaded components: 5-10nH per lead. SMD components: 0.5-2nH. Transformer leakage inductance: typically 1-5% of magnetizing inductance, measured with the secondary shorted.

Calculate the voltage spike. At turn-off, the current through the parasitic inductance cannot change instantly. The spike voltage: Vspike = Lpar * di/dt where di/dt is the turn-off speed of the switch. With Lpar = 20nH and di/dt = 1A/ns (100A in 100ns): Vspike = 20V above the bus voltage.

For flyback converters, the leakage inductance energy is the primary spike source. At turn-off, the primary current switches from the MOSFET to the transformer. The magnetizing inductance energy transfers to the secondary, but the leakage inductance energy has no path (secondary does not couple to it) and appears as a spike on the drain: Vspike = Vin + n*Vout + sqrt(Lleak/Coss) * Ipk.
Calculate the total spike energy per cycle: Espike = 0.5 * Lleak * Ipk^2. At 100kHz, the power that must be handled: Pspike = Espike * fsw. This determines the snubber/clamp dissipation.

steps.description: Design an RC (or RCD) turn-off snubber for the main switch to limit the peak voltage and damp the ringing caused by the resonance between parasitic inductance and device capacitance.

inputs.name: parasitic-inductance-map
inputs.desc: Identified parasitic inductances and their values

inputs.name: spike-energy
inputs.desc: Energy to be absorbed per switching cycle

outputs.name: snubber-component-values
outputs.desc: Snubber capacitor value (sized to absorb the spike energy without excessive voltage rise), snubber resistor value (to damp the ringing and dissipate the energy before the next cycle)

outputs.name: snubber-power-dissipation
outputs.desc: Power dissipated in the snubber resistor: Psnub = 0.5 * Cs * Vs^2 * fsw for a capacitor-charge snubber, or Psnub = 0.5 * Lpar * Ipk^2 * fsw for total spike energy

process: For a turn-off snubber (capacitor across the switch, charged through a diode at turn-off and discharged through a resistor at turn-on): size the capacitor to limit the voltage rise. Cs >= Ipk^2 * Lpar / (Vclamp - Vbus)^2 where Vclamp is the maximum allowable drain voltage.

The snubber capacitor must be fully discharged before the next turn-off. The RC time constant must be less than about 1/3 of the on-time: Rs * Cs < D_min / (3 * fsw). This sets the minimum R for a given C.

Calculate the resistor power dissipation. The energy stored in Cs each cycle is E = 0.5 * Cs * Vclamp^2. This is dissipated in Rs during the on-time: Psnub = E * fsw = 0.5 * Cs * Vclamp^2 * fsw. Size the resistor for this power with margin.

For a simple RC snubber (R in series with C, across the switch, no diode): the resistor damps the LC ringing. Optimal damping: Rs = sqrt(Lpar / Coss) for critical damping of the parasitic ring. Cs should be 2-3 times Coss (the switch output capacitance) so the snubber capacitor dominates the resonance.

Evaluate the efficiency impact. A 1W snubber dissipation on a 50W converter is 2% efficiency loss. If the snubber loss exceeds 1-2% of output power, consider: reducing parasitic inductance through better layout, using an active clamp to recover the energy, or accepting the loss if the spike would otherwise destroy the MOSFET.

steps.description: Design an RCD clamp circuit for flyback converter primary to absorb transformer leakage inductance energy and limit the MOSFET drain voltage to a safe level.

inputs.name: snubber-component-values
inputs.desc: RC snubber analysis for comparison

inputs.name: snubber-power-dissipation
inputs.desc: Snubber loss budget

outputs.name: rcd-clamp-design
outputs.desc: Clamp capacitor, resistor, and diode values. Clamp voltage selection as a trade-off between MOSFET voltage stress and clamp power dissipation

outputs.name: clamp-waveform-analysis
outputs.desc: Expected drain voltage waveform showing the clamping action: Vds rises to Vin + N*Vout, overshoots to Vclamp, then decays as the clamp capacitor discharges through the resistor

process: Select the clamp voltage. The MOSFET sees: Vds_max = Vin_max + Vclamp. The reflected output voltage is Vreflected = N * Vout where N is the turns ratio. Set Vclamp = Vreflected * (1 + k) where k = 0.3 to 1.0. Lower k means less clamping dissipation but higher MOSFET voltage stress. With 650V MOSFET: Vclamp_max = 650 * 0.8 - Vin_max (using 80% derating).

Calculate the clamp resistor. The leakage energy per cycle E = 0.5 * Lleak * Ipk^2 is absorbed by the clamp. In steady state, this energy is dissipated in the resistor: Pclamp = E * fsw = 0.5 * Lleak * Ipk^2 * fsw. The resistor value: Rclamp = Vclamp^2 / Pclamp (since the cap charges to Vclamp and the resistor dissipates the energy).

Calculate the clamp capacitor. The capacitor must hold the clamp voltage approximately constant during the energy absorption (low ripple). Voltage ripple: delta_V = Ipk * Lleak / (Cclamp * Vclamp). For less than 5% ripple: Cclamp > 20 * Ipk * Lleak / (Vclamp * delta_V). Typical values: 1nF to 100nF depending on power level.

Select the clamp diode. It must block Vin + Vclamp in the off state. It must be fast enough (trr < 50ns) to conduct the leakage current spike without allowing excessive voltage overshoot. Ultra-fast recovery or SiC Schottky diodes are preferred. Forward voltage drop adds to the clamp voltage: account for Vf in the clamp voltage calculation.

Optimize the clamp voltage. Plot: MOSFET voltage stress vs clamp voltage, clamp power dissipation vs clamp voltage, and total system efficiency vs clamp voltage. The optimum is where reducing Vclamp further causes diminishing efficiency gain but rapidly increases MOSFET voltage stress. For most flyback designs, Vclamp = 1.3 to 1.5 times the reflected voltage is a good starting point.

steps.description: Design an active clamp circuit that recovers the leakage energy instead of dissipating it, improving efficiency at the cost of added complexity and an auxiliary switch.

inputs.name: rcd-clamp-design
inputs.desc: Passive clamp design for comparison

inputs.name: clamp-waveform-analysis
inputs.desc: Drain voltage waveform and energy analysis

outputs.name: active-clamp-topology
outputs.desc: Active clamp circuit: auxiliary MOSFET and capacitor placement (high-side or low-side), auxiliary switch timing, and resonant transition for ZVS

outputs.name: efficiency-improvement
outputs.desc: Quantified efficiency gain from energy recovery: Pclamp_recovered vs Pclamp_dissipated in RCD, minus the additional switching loss of the auxiliary switch

process: Choose active clamp configuration. High-side: auxiliary MOSFET and clamp cap from drain to Vin+. The clamp cap voltage equals the reflected voltage plus leakage overshoot. Low-side: from source to ground. High-side is more common for flyback because it naturally integrates with the reset mechanism.

Size the clamp capacitor for the active clamp. It must be large enough that its voltage does not change significantly during the leakage energy transfer: Cclamp >> Lleak * Ipk^2 / Vclamp^2. Typical: 10x the value used for an RCD clamp, since the energy is stored (not dissipated) and voltage stability matters.

Design the auxiliary switch timing. After the main switch turns off, the leakage inductance current charges the drain node. When the drain reaches the clamp voltage, the auxiliary MOSFET body diode conducts. The controller turns on the auxiliary MOSFET (ZVS turn-on, since the body diode is already conducting). The leakage energy transfers to the clamp capacitor. Before the main switch turns on, the auxiliary switch turns off, and the clamp cap energy resonates with the leakage inductance to discharge the main MOSFET drain capacitance, achieving ZVS on the main switch.

Calculate the ZVS condition. The energy stored in the clamp capacitor must be sufficient to discharge the main MOSFET Coss: 0.5 * Cclamp * Vclamp^2 > 0.5 * Coss * Vds^2. Since Cclamp >> Coss, this is usually satisfied. The resonant period: Tres = 2*pi*sqrt(Lleak * Coss). The dead time between auxiliary off and main on must be Tres/4 for the drain to reach zero.

Quantify the efficiency gain. The RCD clamp dissipates Pclamp = 0.5 * Lleak * Ipk^2 * fsw in heat. The active clamp recovers this energy (returns it to the input or output). Subtract the auxiliary MOSFET gate drive loss and any conduction loss during the clamp period. Net gain is typically 1-3% at full load for converters with significant leakage inductance.

steps.description: Compare snubber and clamp options, select the best approach for the application, verify the design through simulation or bench measurement, and finalize component specifications.

inputs.name: active-clamp-topology
inputs.desc: Active clamp design if applicable

inputs.name: efficiency-improvement
inputs.desc: Efficiency comparison between clamp approaches

outputs.name: selected-snubber-design
outputs.desc: Final snubber or clamp design with complete component specifications: part numbers, voltage ratings with derating, power ratings, and PCB placement requirements

outputs.name: verification-results
outputs.desc: Simulated or measured drain voltage waveform with the snubber installed, confirming peak voltage is within the MOSFET safe operating area with margin

process: Compare the options. Simple RC snubber: lowest cost, adequate for low-power designs where snubber loss is under 1% of output. RCD clamp: standard for flyback under 100W, easy to design and reliable. Active clamp: justified when leakage loss exceeds 2-3% of output power, typically for higher-power flyback or forward converters.
