For the selected design, verify with SPICE simulation. Model the parasitic inductances, MOSFET Coss (nonlinear, use the manufacturer's SPICE model), and the snubber/clamp components. Simulate the turn-off transient and verify: peak Vds < 80% of MOSFET rated voltage, ringing decays within 20% of the switching period, no sustained oscillation.

If bench prototyping: measure the drain voltage with a high-bandwidth probe (>200MHz bandwidth, use a ground spring not a 6-inch ground lead). Start without the snubber to characterize the spike. Add snubber components and verify suppression. Iterate on R and C values if needed.

Select specific components. Snubber capacitor: film or ceramic, with voltage rating > 2x peak voltage for reliability. The capacitor must handle the RMS current: Irms = Cs * Vclamp * fsw (roughly). Select a capacitor rated for this ripple current. Snubber resistor: use a film resistor rated for pulse energy, not just average power. Carbon composition handles pulses better than thin-film.

Document the final design: schematic, component BOM with ratings and derating, expected power dissipation, thermal placement (snubber resistor may need heat sinking or PCB copper area for cooling), and the measured/simulated drain waveform as verification evidence.

description: Select power MOSFETs for switching converter applications by analyzing conduction and switching losses, thermal performance, figure of merit, parallel operation, and wide-bandgap (GaN, SiC) trade-offs against silicon.

steps.description: Calculate conduction and switching losses for candidate MOSFETs at the converter operating point, accounting for temperature effects and gate drive conditions.

inputs.name: converter-requirements
inputs.desc: Drain-source voltage, RMS and peak current, switching frequency, gate drive voltage, and operating ambient temperature

inputs.name: candidate-datasheets
inputs.desc: Datasheets for 3-5 candidate MOSFETs with Rds(on), Qg, Qgd, Coss, turn-on/turn-off times, and thermal resistance

outputs.name: conduction-loss-comparison
outputs.desc: Pcond = Irms^2 * Rds(on) at operating junction temperature for each candidate, noting the Rds(on) temperature coefficient

outputs.name: switching-loss-comparison
outputs.desc: Psw for each candidate: turn-on loss (including diode reverse recovery), turn-off loss, and Coss-related loss at the operating voltage and current

process: Calculate Rds(on) at operating temperature. The datasheet specifies Rds(on) at 25C. The temperature coefficient is positive: Rds(on)(T) = Rds(on)(25) * (T/300)^2.3 approximately. At 100C, Rds(on) is roughly 1.7x the 25C value. Use the operating Tj, not ambient, for this calculation.

Calculate conduction loss: Pcond = Irms^2 * Rds(on)(Tj). For a buck converter, Irms = Iout * sqrt(D). For the freewheeling MOSFET (synchronous rectifier), Irms = Iout * sqrt(1-D). Include body diode conduction during dead time if applicable.

Estimate switching loss from datasheet waveforms. Turn-on: the MOSFET charges through the Miller plateau while simultaneously carrying the inductor current and supporting the bus voltage. Energy per turn-on event: Eon = 0.5 * Vds * Id * (tri + tfv) where tri is the current rise time and tfv is the voltage fall time. These depend on gate drive strength: tri = Qgs2 / Ig, tfv = Qgd / Ig.

Turn-off: reverse of turn-on. Eoff = 0.5 * Vds * Id * (trv + tfi). Additionally, the Coss must be charged from near zero to Vds: Ecoss = integral(Vds * Coss(Vds) dVds) from 0 to Vds. This energy is dissipated in the switch at the next turn-on (hard switching) or recovered (soft switching).

Include reverse recovery of the complementary diode. When the high-side MOSFET turns on in a synchronous buck, the low-side body diode reverse recovery adds to the turn-on loss: Prr = Qrr * Vds * fsw. Si MOSFETs: Qrr can be significant (50-200nC). GaN: no reverse recovery (no p-n body diode).

steps.description: Compare MOSFET candidates using the appropriate figure of merit for the application: Rds(on) * Qg for hard-switching, Rds(on) * Qoss for soft-switching, and Rds(on) * Area for power density.

inputs.name: conduction-loss-comparison
inputs.desc: Conduction loss for each candidate

inputs.name: switching-loss-comparison
inputs.desc: Switching loss breakdown for each candidate

outputs.name: fom-ranking
outputs.desc: Candidates ranked by the relevant figure of merit, with total loss (Pcond + Psw) calculated at the operating point

outputs.name: loss-dominant-mode
outputs.desc: Whether the application is conduction-loss-dominant (low fsw, high current) or switching-loss-dominant (high fsw, high voltage), which determines which FOM matters most

process: Calculate Rds(on) * Qg for each candidate. This is the classic hard-switching FOM. Lower is better. It captures the fundamental trade-off: lower Rds(on) requires a larger die (more Qg), so a better FOM means better silicon technology, not just a bigger chip.

For soft-switching applications (resonant converters, ZVS), use Rds(on) * Qoss. The switching loss depends on the output charge (energy stored in Coss) rather than the gate charge. GaN devices excel here because their Qoss is much lower than Si at the same Rds(on).

Determine the loss-dominant mode. At low switching frequencies (under 100kHz) with high currents: conduction loss dominates, so select for lowest Rds(on) even if Qg is high. At high switching frequencies (above 300kHz) or high voltage: switching loss dominates, so select for lowest Qg and Qgd even if Rds(on) is slightly higher.

Plot total loss vs Rds(on) for each technology. For Si MOSFETs: the Rds(on) * Qg trade-off means there is an optimum die size (too small = high conduction loss, too large = high switching loss). Calculate the optimum: d(Ptotal)/d(Rds(on)) = 0 gives the ideal Rds(on) for minimum total loss at a given fsw.
Rank the candidates by total power loss at the actual operating point. The FOM is a screening tool; the actual loss calculation at the specific operating conditions is the final decision criterion.

steps.description: Evaluate whether GaN or SiC devices offer meaningful advantages over silicon for the application, considering performance, cost, gate drive complexity, and reliability maturity.

inputs.name: fom-ranking
inputs.desc: Silicon MOSFET candidates ranked by FOM and total loss

inputs.name: loss-dominant-mode
inputs.desc: Whether conduction or switching loss dominates

outputs.name: wbg-assessment
outputs.desc: Quantified comparison: GaN vs SiC vs Si at the operating point, including total loss, required heat sink size, and achievable switching frequency for each technology

outputs.name: technology-recommendation
outputs.desc: Recommended semiconductor technology with cost-performance trade-off analysis: $/Watt saved, break-even volume, and supply chain availability

process: GaN HEMT evaluation. GaN devices (e-mode, 650V class) have: zero reverse recovery (no body diode), very low Qg and Qgd (5-10x lower than Si), low Rds(on) * Qg FOM. Best for: applications above 200kHz where switching loss dominates, half-bridge topologies where reverse recovery is significant, and designs targeting high power density.

GaN challenges: gate voltage is limited to 6V (vs 20V for Si), requiring precise gate drive. No avalanche rating (unlike Si which can absorb transient overvoltage). Threshold voltage is low (1.2-1.7V), making Miller turn-on prevention critical. Packages are often QFN with exposed die-attach pad, requiring specific soldering profiles.

SiC MOSFET evaluation. SiC (1200V class and above) offers: very low Rds(on) at high voltage (10x better than Si at 1200V), high temperature operation (175C junction), fast body diode with low Qrr, high avalanche ruggedness. Best for: 600V+ applications (PFC, solar inverter, EV charger, motor drives), high-temperature environments.

SiC challenges: gate oxide reliability requires -5V to +18V gate drive (not 0 to 12V like Si). Higher cost per amp than Si (3-5x at equivalent current rating). Threshold voltage instability under bias-temperature stress. Requires negative turn-off voltage to prevent parasitic turn-on from dv/dt.

Cost-performance trade-off. Calculate the efficiency difference: delta_eta = (Ploss_Si - Ploss_WBG) / Pout. Calculate the annual energy savings at a given duty cycle and electricity cost. Calculate the heat sink size reduction. If the WBG device eliminates a heat sink ($5-20) or allows removing a fan ($3-10), include that system-level cost reduction. Break-even: if the WBG device costs $3 more but saves $5 in heat sink and fan, it is immediately cost-effective.

steps.description: Design parallel MOSFET configurations for high-current applications, addressing current sharing during static and dynamic operation, gate drive distribution, and layout symmetry.

inputs.name: wbg-assessment
inputs.desc: Technology selection (Si, GaN, or SiC)

inputs.name: technology-recommendation
inputs.desc: Selected device and its ratings vs application requirements

outputs.name: parallel-configuration
outputs.desc: Number of parallel MOSFETs, gate drive distribution method, and current derating factor for the paralleled group

outputs.name: layout-symmetry-requirements
outputs.desc: PCB layout rules for balanced current sharing: matched trace lengths, symmetric gate resistor placement, thermal coupling between devices

process: Determine the number of parallel devices. The total Rds(on) of N parallel MOSFETs: Rds(on)_total = Rds(on)_single / N. Size N so that conduction loss and thermal dissipation per device are within the single-device rating with derating. Apply a 10-20% current derating to account for mismatch.

Static current sharing. Si MOSFETs share current well in steady state because Rds(on) has a positive temperature coefficient: the hotter device has higher resistance and carries less current, creating a self-balancing mechanism. Mismatch from Rds(on) tolerance (typically +/-20% for production parts) causes the worst-case device to carry 1.2x the average current.

Dynamic current sharing. During switching transitions, current imbalance is caused by: unequal gate drive impedance (different trace lengths = different L), unequal source inductance (current sense effect), and device parameter spread (Vth, Qg). The device that turns on first carries the full current briefly, causing localized heating.

Gate drive for parallel MOSFETs. Option 1: individual gate resistors from a single driver. Each MOSFET gets its own Rg (typically 1-10 ohms) to prevent oscillation between the parallel gates. The driver must source N times the gate charge. Option 2: dedicated driver per MOSFET (for 4+ parallel devices). This isolates the gate loops and gives better control.

Layout for parallel MOSFETs. Matched trace lengths from driver to each gate within 10%. Symmetric placement of drain and source connections so each device sees the same commutation loop inductance. Place devices close together on the same heat sink for thermal coupling. Common-source inductance (current sensing): if each MOSFET has its own Kelvin source, connect them individually to the driver return; if not, use a common source connection with minimal inductance.

steps.description: Verify the selected MOSFET against its safe operating area under all conditions including avalanche, linear mode, and short circuit, then finalize the component selection with part number and second source.

inputs.name: parallel-configuration
inputs.desc: Parallel MOSFET configuration if applicable

inputs.name: layout-symmetry-requirements
inputs.desc: Layout constraints for the selected configuration

outputs.name: soa-verification
outputs.desc: Safe operating area verification at worst-case: Vds vs Id point plotted against the SOA curves for DC and pulsed operation, confirming the operating point is within bounds

outputs.name: final-mosfet-selection
outputs.desc: Selected MOSFET part number with key parameters, second-source alternatives, and package selection rationale (thermal, size, parasitic)

process: Plot the operating point on the SOA diagram. The SOA shows the maximum Vds vs Id for DC, 10ms, 1ms, 100us, and single-pulse operation. During normal hard switching, the MOSFET traverses the full Vds range while carrying Id (the switching trajectory). This trajectory must stay within the 100us or shorter pulse boundary.

Check avalanche rating for unclamped inductive switching (UIS). If the MOSFET can see voltage spikes exceeding its Vds rating (e.g., from parasitic inductance without adequate snubbing), it must survive avalanche. The avalanche energy rating EAS from the datasheet must exceed the energy in the parasitic inductance: EAS > 0.5 * Lpar * Ipk^2 * (Vds_rated / (Vds_rated - Vbus)).

For linear-mode operation (hot-swap, inrush limiting): the MOSFET operates in the active region with both high Vds and high Id simultaneously. Check the SOA curves carefully, as silicon MOSFETs can suffer from thermal instability (current crowding) at high Vds in linear mode. Use a SOA-rated MOSFET if linear-mode operation exceeds 1ms.

Package selection. TO-220: through-hole, excellent thermal path to heat sink, high parasitic inductance. D2PAK: SMD equivalent of TO-220. QFN/PQFN: lowest parasitics (0.5nH vs 5-10nH for leaded), best for high-frequency (above 500kHz). LFPAK: low inductance, high current density. Select based on the thermal, parasitic inductance, and assembly requirements.

Finalize: record the primary part number, its key parameters (Vds, Rds(on) at 25C and 100C, Qg, Qgd, Rth_jc, package), at least one second-source alternative from a different manufacturer, and any application notes from the manufacturer for the selected topology.

description: Design a battery management system covering cell chemistry characterization, cell balancing, state of charge estimation (coulomb counting, OCV, Kalman filter), protection circuits, and pack-level thermal management.

steps.description: Characterize the selected cell chemistry to establish voltage curves, impedance model, capacity, and thermal behavior that drive all BMS design decisions.

inputs.name: cell-selection
inputs.desc: Selected cell: chemistry (LFP, NMC, NCA, LTO), form factor (cylindrical, pouch, prismatic), capacity (Ah), and nominal voltage

inputs.name: application-requirements
inputs.desc: Pack voltage, energy (kWh), peak current, operating temperature range, and cycle life target

outputs.name: cell-model
outputs.desc: Equivalent circuit model: OCV(SOC) lookup table, series resistance Rs, RC pairs for transient response (R1/C1 for fast dynamics, R2/C2 for slow diffusion), all as functions of SOC and temperature

outputs.name: operating-limits
outputs.desc: Cell operating limits: max/min voltage per chemistry (4.2V/2.5V for NMC, 3.65V/2.0V for LFP), max continuous and peak discharge current, max charge current vs temperature (CCCP curve), temperature limits

process: Characterize the OCV-SOC relationship. Fully charge the cell, rest for 2+ hours (to reach equilibrium), then discharge in 5% SOC increments with 1-hour rest periods between each step. Record the rested voltage at each SOC point. Repeat at 0C, 25C, and 45C. The resulting OCV(SOC, T) table is the foundation of SOC estimation.

Measure the impedance model. Apply pulse discharge tests: 10-second current pulses at C/5, 1C, and 3C rates at each SOC point. From the voltage response: the immediate voltage drop gives Rs (series resistance). The exponential recovery gives R1/C1 (fast dynamics, tau = 1-10s) and R2/C2 (slow diffusion, tau = 100-1000s).

Document the capacity vs temperature: at 0C, capacity may be 70-80% of the 25C rating. At -20C, as low as 50%. The charge acceptance also drops dramatically at low temperature (lithium plating risk). Record the maximum charge rate vs temperature: at 0C, most cells limit to 0.1C-0.2C charge rate.

Characterize the cycle life degradation. The capacity fade model: C(n) = C(0) * (1 - k * n^0.5) where n is the cycle count and k is an empirical constant depending on depth of discharge, charge rate, and temperature. LFP at 80% DOD: 3000+ cycles to 80% capacity. NMC at 80% DOD: 1000-2000 cycles. High temperature accelerates degradation (roughly doubles for each 10C increase).
Compile the complete cell model: OCV table, impedance parameters, capacity vs temperature, charge rate limits vs temperature, and cycle life curves. This is the input to the BMS algorithm design.

steps.description: Design the cell balancing system to equalize state of charge across series-connected cells, choosing between passive (dissipative) and active (energy-transfer) balancing based on mismatch magnitude and efficiency requirements.

inputs.name: cell-model
inputs.desc: Cell equivalent circuit model with OCV-SOC curves

inputs.name: operating-limits
inputs.desc: Cell voltage and current limits

outputs.name: balancing-method
outputs.desc: Selected balancing approach (passive resistive, active capacitor shuttle, active inductor, or transformer-based) with rationale based on mismatch magnitude and application

outputs.name: balancing-circuit-design
outputs.desc: Circuit schematic: balancing resistor value and MOSFET switch for passive, or inductor/capacitor and switching topology for active, with control thresholds and balancing current

process: Assess the mismatch magnitude. New cells from the same batch typically mismatch by 1-3% SOC. After aging, mismatch can grow to 5-10% as cells degrade at different rates. The balancing system must correct this mismatch within a reasonable time (typically during charging, over 1-4 hours).

Passive (dissipative) balancing: a resistor and MOSFET switch across each cell. The BMS turns on the switch for the highest-voltage cell(s) to discharge them through the resistor until all cells are equalized. Balancing current: Ibal = Vcell / Rbal. Typical: 50-200mA. Time to balance 5% SOC mismatch on a 3Ah cell: delta_Q = 0.05 * 3Ah = 150mAh. At 100mA: 1.5 hours. Dissipation: Pbal = Vcell * Ibal = 3.6V * 100mA = 360mW per cell.

Active balancing: transfers energy from high cells to low cells instead of dissipating it. Capacitor shuttle: a capacitor switches between adjacent cells, transferring charge from higher to lower. Inductor-based: uses a small inductor to move energy between cells with a boost/buck converter per cell pair. Transformer-based: a multi-winding transformer allows any-cell-to-any-cell transfer.

Selection criteria: for small packs (under 16 cells) with small mismatch: passive is preferred for its simplicity and low cost ($0.10-0.50 per cell in components). For large packs (EV, grid storage) or where energy efficiency matters: active balancing recovers the energy and can balance faster with higher currents. The added complexity and cost ($2-5 per cell) must be justified by the application.

Design the control algorithm. For passive: turn on the balancing MOSFET when the cell voltage exceeds the average by more than a threshold (typically 10-20mV). Turn off when equalized within 5mV. For active: run the transfer when any cell pair has more than 20mV difference. Stop when within 5mV. Log the balancing activity as a health indicator (increasing imbalance suggests a weak cell).

steps.description: Implement state of charge estimation using coulomb counting, OCV lookup, and Kalman filter fusion to achieve accurate SOC under all operating conditions.

inputs.name: balancing-method
inputs.desc: Cell balancing approach (affects per-cell monitoring requirements)

inputs.name: balancing-circuit-design
inputs.desc: Balancing circuit with current sensor placement

outputs.name: soc-algorithm
outputs.desc: SOC estimation algorithm specification: coulomb counting with OCV correction at rest periods, and extended Kalman filter for continuous estimation during operation

outputs.name: sensor-requirements
outputs.desc: Current sensor accuracy (hall effect, shunt resistor + amplifier), voltage measurement resolution, temperature sensor placement and accuracy

process: Implement coulomb counting as the baseline: SOC(t) = SOC(t0) + (1/Qnom) * integral(I * eta_c * dt) from t0 to t. Where eta_c is the coulombic efficiency (~99.5% for lithium-ion charge, 100% for discharge). The integral accumulates current over time. Error sources: current measurement offset (even 10mA offset accumulates to 0.24Ah per day), and capacity (Qnom) uncertainty.

Add OCV-based correction. When the pack rests for 30+ minutes (current near zero, voltage settling), read the cell voltage and look up SOC from the OCV(SOC) table. Reset the coulomb counter to this value. For LFP chemistry: the OCV curve is very flat from 20-80% SOC (only 50mV change), making OCV-based estimation poor in the middle range. For NMC: the OCV curve has better slope throughout.

Implement the extended Kalman filter (EKF). State vector: [SOC, V_rc1, V_rc2]. Measurement: terminal voltage Vt = OCV(SOC) - I*Rs - V_rc1 - V_rc2. Process model: SOC(k+1) = SOC(k) - (dt*I)/(3600*Qnom), V_rc1(k+1) = V_rc1(k)*exp(-dt/tau1) + R1*I*(1-exp(-dt/tau1)). The EKF fuses the coulomb counting (process model) with voltage measurement (observation model), weighting them by their respective noise covariances.

Tune the EKF. Process noise Q reflects confidence in coulomb counting: higher Q = more weight on voltage measurement. Measurement noise R reflects voltage sensor accuracy and model error. Start with Q = diag([1e-6, 1e-4, 1e-4]) and R = [1e-4] and tune against test data. The EKF should converge to within 3% SOC error within 10 minutes of operation regardless of initial SOC guess.

Specify the sensors. Current measurement: shunt resistor with instrumentation amplifier (accuracy 0.1-0.5% of reading) or hall-effect sensor (1-3% accuracy but galvanic isolation). Voltage measurement: the BMS monitor IC (e.g., LTC6813, MAX17853) measures each cell voltage to 1-2mV accuracy. Temperature: NTC thermistor per cell group, accuracy +/-1C, placed on the cell surface midway between tabs.

steps.description: Design the hardware protection circuits for overvoltage, undervoltage, overcurrent, over-temperature, and short circuit, with response times and fault handling hierarchy.

inputs.name: soc-algorithm
inputs.desc: SOC estimation method and measurement infrastructure

inputs.name: sensor-requirements
inputs.desc: Sensor specifications and placement

outputs.name: protection-circuit-schematic
outputs.desc: Hardware protection schematic: comparators or dedicated protection IC, MOSFET disconnect switches (charge and discharge paths), pre-charge circuit, and fault indicator outputs

outputs.name: protection-thresholds
outputs.desc: Threshold table: OVP trip and release voltages, UVP trip and release, OCP instantaneous and delayed, OTP warning and shutdown, with hysteresis values and response times

process: Overvoltage protection (OVP). Threshold: cell chemistry maximum (4.20V for NMC, 3.65V for LFP) plus a small margin for measurement accuracy. Response: when any cell exceeds OVP, disconnect the charge path MOSFET. Do not disconnect the discharge path (the pack can still be used). Hysteresis: release at OVP - 50mV to prevent oscillation. Response time: under 100ms from the monitor IC, or under 1us from a hardware comparator for safety-critical backup.

Undervoltage protection (UVP). Threshold: 2.5V for NMC, 2.0V for LFP. Below these voltages, copper dissolution occurs (irreversible damage). Response: disconnect the discharge path MOSFET. Allow charging to recover. If a cell is below 1.5V, it may be damaged and should not be charged without a low-current recovery protocol.

Overcurrent protection (OCP). Two levels: software OCP from the BMS microcontroller (response in 1-10ms, configurable threshold) and hardware OCP from a comparator on the current sense signal (response in microseconds, fixed threshold at the absolute maximum). Short circuit protection: detect a current spike above 5-10x rated current within 10us and disconnect both charge and discharge MOSFETs.

Pre-charge circuit. When connecting the pack to a discharged load (large capacitor on the bus), the inrush current can exceed OCP. A pre-charge resistor in series with a bypass MOSFET limits the inrush: Rpre = Vpack / Ipre_max. Pre-charge time: t = -R*C*ln(1 - Vpre_target/Vpack). After the load voltage reaches 90% of pack voltage, close the main contactor and open the pre-charge path.

Over-temperature protection. NTC thermistors on each cell group feed into the BMS. Warning threshold: 45-50C (reduce charge current). Shutdown threshold: 60C (disconnect both paths). Under-temperature: below 0C, disable charging (lithium plating risk). Allow discharge down to -20C at reduced current. Log all protection events with timestamp, cell voltages, and temperatures for post-incident analysis.

steps.description: Design the pack-level thermal management system to keep cells within their operating temperature range, using thermal modeling, cooling path design, and heating for cold-start conditions.

inputs.name: protection-circuit-schematic
inputs.desc: Protection circuits with temperature sensor placement

inputs.name: protection-thresholds
inputs.desc: Temperature thresholds for warning and shutdown

outputs.name: thermal-management-design
outputs.desc: Cooling/heating system: air-cooled (fan sizing, duct design) or liquid-cooled (cold plate, coolant flow rate, pump sizing), plus PTC heater for cold-start pre-heating

outputs.name: temperature-uniformity-analysis
outputs.desc: Predicted temperature variation across the pack: maximum cell-to-cell temperature difference (target less than 5C to minimize aging mismatch), hot spot identification, and thermal runaway containment measures

process: Calculate the heat generation rate. Each cell dissipates: Pcell = I^2 * Rint + Pside_reactions. Rint is the total internal resistance at the operating SOC and temperature. At 1C discharge for a 50Ah cell with 2 milliohm internal resistance: Pcell = 50^2 * 0.002 = 5W. For the full pack: Ptotal = N_cells * Pcell.

Air cooling design. Forced air: size the fan for the required airflow. The temperature rise of the cooling air: delta_T_air = Ptotal / (m_dot * cp_air). For 200W total dissipation and 5C air temperature rise: m_dot = 200 / (5 * 1005) = 0.04 kg/s = 33 CFM. Duct the air across the cells for uniform cooling. The cells nearest the air inlet run coolest; stagger the airflow path to reduce the temperature gradient.

Liquid cooling design. A cold plate under or between cells with coolant (water-glycol) flowing through channels. The thermal resistance from cell surface to coolant: Rth = 1/(h*A) where h depends on flow rate and channel geometry. Size the pump for the pressure drop through the cold plate. Typical: 5-10 LPM for a 10kWh pack. Liquid cooling provides much lower temperature gradients (under 3C across the pack) compared to air (5-10C).

Cold-start heating. Below 0C, charge current must be limited. A PTC heater (self-regulating, cannot overheat) warms the cells before charging. Size: the heater must bring the coldest cell above 5C within the target time. Energy: Q = m_cells * cp_cell * delta_T. For a 10kg pack of cells (cp ~ 1000 J/(kg*K)) heated 20C: Q = 200kJ. At 500W heater power: 400 seconds (6.7 minutes).

Thermal runaway containment. If one cell enters thermal runaway (internal short, venting, fire), the design must prevent propagation to adjacent cells. Measures: thermal barriers (aerogel, mica) between cells, vent paths to direct hot gases away from other cells, cell spacing to limit radiative heat transfer, and fuses or disconnect switches to isolate the faulted cell. Test per UL 2580 or IEC 62619 to verify no propagation.

description: Measure power supply performance using proper oscilloscope probing, current measurement techniques, ripple and noise measurement methodology, efficiency characterization, and impedance analysis with a network analyzer.

steps.description: Select the correct oscilloscope probes for power supply measurements, understanding bandwidth limitations, loading effects, and the critical importance of probe grounding technique.

inputs.name: measurement-objectives
inputs.desc: What needs to be measured: output ripple, switching node voltage, gate drive waveform, current waveform, with expected voltage and frequency ranges

inputs.name: available-equipment
inputs.desc: Oscilloscope bandwidth and channel count, available probes (passive 10x, passive 1x, active differential, current probes)

outputs.name: probe-assignment
outputs.desc: Probe type assigned to each measurement point with rationale: bandwidth requirement, voltage range, common-mode rejection needs, and loading considerations

outputs.name: grounding-method
outputs.desc: Grounding method for each measurement: ground spring (tip-and-barrel) for ripple, standard ground clip for low-frequency, differential probe for high-side signals

process: For switching node voltage (fast transitions, 5-100ns edges, high voltage): use a standard 10x passive probe (500MHz bandwidth typical). The 10x attenuation reduces loading. The 10:1 ratio gives adequate resolution for signals above 1V. For GaN and SiC converters with sub-10ns edges, use a 500MHz+ active probe.

For output voltage ripple (millivolt-level AC riding on a DC rail): use a 1x passive probe or an active probe for maximum sensitivity. The scope must be AC-coupled or use the math channel (Ch1 - DC_offset) to see the millivolts of ripple on a multi-volt DC rail. Bandwidth-limit the scope to 20MHz to exclude high-frequency noise that is not true ripple.

Critical: ground lead technique. The standard 6-inch alligator ground clip adds 5-10nH of inductance, which creates a resonant antenna with the probe tip capacitance. At 100MHz, this picks up switching noise and adds 50-200mV of artifact. For ripple measurement, this artifact drowns the real signal. Use the tip-and-barrel method: remove the ground clip and use a short ground spring or bare wire soldered to a ground point within 5mm of the measurement point.

For high-side measurements (referenced to a switching node, not ground): use a differential probe. It has two inputs (+ and -) and rejects the common-mode voltage. Required CMRR: at 100V common mode and 10mV desired resolution, need >80dB CMRR. High-voltage differential probes (Tektronix, Teledyne LeCroy) provide 100:1 attenuation and >1kV common-mode range.

For gate drive waveforms: use a differential probe referenced to the MOSFET source (not circuit ground) to see the true Vgs. This is especially critical for high-side gate drive and for measuring Miller plateau and gate ringing. A standard probe referenced to circuit ground will show Vgs + source inductance noise.

steps.description: Select and apply the correct current measurement technique based on the signal characteristics: DC+AC, AC only, peak, bandwidth requirement, and isolation needs.

inputs.name: probe-assignment
inputs.desc: Voltage probe assignments for correlated measurements

inputs.name: grounding-method
inputs.desc: Grounding approach for each measurement point

outputs.name: current-sensor-selection
outputs.desc: Current sensor type for each measurement: shunt + differential amp (highest accuracy), Rogowski coil (AC only, wide bandwidth), current transformer (AC, galvanic isolation), or hall-effect clamp (DC+AC, moderate bandwidth)

outputs.name: current-measurement-setup
outputs.desc: Complete measurement setup: sensor placement on the PCB, deskew with voltage channel, and calibration check procedure

process: Shunt resistor with differential probe: the highest-accuracy method. Place a low-inductance shunt (1-10 milliohm, 4-terminal Kelvin) in the current path. Measure the voltage across it with a differential probe. Current = V_shunt / R_shunt. Accuracy limited by shunt tolerance (0.1-1%), temperature coefficient, and probe accuracy. Bandwidth: limited by the probe (up to 200MHz with an active differential probe).

Rogowski coil: AC current only (no DC component). A flexible coil wraps around the conductor. The output voltage is proportional to di/dt, so an integrator is needed (usually built into the probe). Bandwidth: 30MHz+ for good probes. Dynamic range: from milliamps to kiloamps. Non-invasive (does not require breaking the circuit). Best for: measuring switch current during transitions, transformer current, and high di/dt events.

Current transformer (CT): AC current, galvanically isolated. A toroidal core with a secondary winding around the conductor. The secondary current = Iprimary / N (turns ratio). Measure the secondary current through a burden resistor. Droop at low frequency: the CT saturates if the current has a DC component or the pulse width exceeds the L/R time constant. Not suitable for continuous DC measurement.

Hall-effect current probe (clamp-on): measures DC and AC current. Bandwidth: typically 50-100MHz for split-core probes, up to 120MHz for high-end. Accuracy: 1-3% of reading. Degaussing required before precision measurement (residual magnetization offsets the zero). Best for: measuring average inductor current, load current, and input current where DC component matters.

Deskew: when measuring voltage and current simultaneously (for power loss calculation), the time alignment between channels must be verified. Use a deskew fixture or measure a known circuit (resistor with fast current step) and adjust the channel delay until V and I edges align. A 2ns skew at 100MHz causes significant power measurement error.

steps.description: Measure output voltage ripple and noise using proper technique to separate switching-frequency ripple from high-frequency noise and random noise, producing a specification-grade measurement.

inputs.name: current-sensor-selection
inputs.desc: Current measurement setup for correlated ripple analysis

inputs.name: current-measurement-setup
inputs.desc: Complete current measurement configuration

outputs.name: ripple-measurement
outputs.desc: Switching-frequency ripple: peak-to-peak and RMS at fundamental and harmonics, measured with 20MHz bandwidth limit per industry standard. Separation of capacitive (ESR) and inductive (ESL) contributions

outputs.name: noise-measurement
outputs.desc: High-frequency noise components: common-mode spikes, ringing at switching transitions, broadband noise floor. Measured with full probe bandwidth to characterize the complete output spectrum

process: Set up the measurement. AC couple the oscilloscope (or use DC couple and math subtract the DC offset). Use a 1x probe or active probe for maximum sensitivity. Apply the tip-and-barrel grounding technique. Place the probe tip and ground directly across the output capacitor terminals or the load terminals (these may differ due to PCB trace impedance).

Measure switching-frequency ripple. Set the scope bandwidth limit to 20MHz. This is the industry standard (per JESD22-A, Mil-Std-461) and removes high-frequency spikes that are not true output ripple. Measure peak-to-peak voltage. The ripple waveform shape reveals its source: triangular ripple = ESR * delta_IL (capacitor ESR driven), sawtooth with spikes = ESL * di/dt at the switching transitions (capacitor ESL driven).

Measure high-frequency noise. Remove the 20MHz bandwidth limit. The full-bandwidth measurement shows switching transition spikes (typically 10-100ns duration, 10-200mV amplitude) and ringing. These are caused by parasitic inductance in the output capacitor and PCB traces ringing with parasitic capacitance. Quantify the spike amplitude and ringing frequency.

Frequency-domain analysis. Use the scope FFT function or transfer the waveform to a PC for spectrum analysis. The ripple spectrum shows peaks at fsw and its harmonics (2*fsw, 3*fsw, etc.). The noise floor between harmonics indicates random noise. The spectrum is useful for identifying specific noise sources and verifying filter effectiveness.

Load transient test. Step the load from 10% to 90% of rated current and measure the output voltage excursion. The initial spike (within the first switching cycle) is determined by output capacitance ESR and ESL. The droop/overshoot after the spike is determined by the control loop bandwidth. Measure both the spike amplitude and the settling time to within the regulation band.

steps.description: Measure converter efficiency accurately across the load range, addressing measurement instrument accuracy, thermal equilibrium, and light-load measurement challenges.

inputs.name: ripple-measurement
inputs.desc: Output ripple characterization for output power accuracy

inputs.name: noise-measurement
inputs.desc: Noise characterization

outputs.name: efficiency-curve
outputs.desc: Measured efficiency vs load current from 1% to 100% of rated load, at minimum, nominal, and maximum input voltage, after thermal equilibrium at each point

outputs.name: loss-budget-verification
outputs.desc: Measured total loss compared to the predicted loss budget, with discrepancy analysis identifying unaccounted losses

process: Select measurement instruments. Power analyzer (Yokogawa, Keysight): best accuracy (0.01-0.05% of reading), true RMS measurement including ripple and harmonics. Digital multimeters: 6.5-digit DMMs provide 0.01% accuracy for DC voltage and current, adequate for steady-state measurements. Oscilloscope: not recommended for efficiency (limited vertical resolution and DC accuracy).

Input power: measure Vin and Iin simultaneously. For DC-DC converters, use a shunt and DMM for current, and a separate DMM for voltage, at the converter input terminals (not the power supply terminals, to include cable losses). For AC-DC, use a power analyzer that handles power factor and THD.

Output power: measure Vout and Iout at the load terminals. Use 4-wire (Kelvin) sensing for both voltage and current to eliminate lead resistance errors. At high current (50A+), cable drops of 100-200mV can cause 0.5-1% efficiency error if not accounted for.

Thermal equilibrium. Efficiency changes with temperature (Rds(on) increases, capacitor ESR changes). Allow 15-30 minutes at each load point for the converter to reach thermal steady state before recording the measurement. Monitor the case temperature of the hottest component; it should stabilize within 1C before the measurement is valid.

Light-load efficiency. At loads below 10% of rated, the quiescent power of the controller IC, gate drive, and bias supplies dominates. Measurement accuracy becomes critical: a 100mA offset in a 10A-rated ammeter causes 1% efficiency error at 1A load but only 0.01% at full load. Use a lower-range meter or power analyzer for light-load measurements. Document the no-load input power (quiescent consumption).

steps.description: Measure the output impedance of the converter and the input impedance of the load using a frequency response analyzer or network analyzer, for stability verification and PDN characterization.

inputs.name: efficiency-curve
inputs.desc: Efficiency data to establish operating points for impedance measurement

inputs.name: loss-budget-verification
inputs.desc: Loss analysis to identify components affecting impedance

outputs.name: output-impedance-plot
outputs.desc: Converter output impedance magnitude and phase vs frequency from 10Hz to 10MHz, showing the closed-loop impedance (with feedback active) and open-loop impedance (feedback disabled)

outputs.name: stability-margin-measurement
outputs.desc: Measured loop gain (using the Middlebrook or Ridley injection method) showing crossover frequency, phase margin, and gain margin under actual operating conditions

process: Output impedance measurement. Inject a small AC current into the output using a signal generator and a wideband current injection transformer. Measure the resulting AC voltage at the output. Zout(f) = Vac_out(f) / Iac_injected(f). Sweep from 10Hz (below the loop bandwidth) to 10MHz (above the switching frequency). The closed-loop output impedance shows the effect of the feedback loop.

Loop gain measurement using voltage injection (Middlebrook method). Break the feedback loop at the output of the error amplifier. Inject a small AC signal in series with the loop. Measure the signals on both sides of the injection point: T(f) = -Vreturn(f) / Vinject(f). The magnitude crossover gives the bandwidth; the phase at crossover gives the phase margin. Use an injection transformer (Picotest J2111A or similar) rated for the frequency range.

Practical considerations: the injection signal must be small enough not to perturb the operating point (typically 10-50mV at the output, or 1-5% of the error amplifier output swing). Too large and the measurement includes nonlinear effects. Too small and the signal-to-noise ratio is poor. Use averaging (64-256 averages) to reduce noise.

Input impedance measurement. Important for verifying the Middlebrook stability criterion with the input filter. Inject AC current at the converter input and measure the AC voltage. The converter input impedance for a regulated converter is negative at low frequency (negative resistance) and transitions to positive impedance at higher frequency. The filter output impedance must remain below this curve.

Compare measured results to design predictions. The crossover frequency should match the compensator design within 20%. Phase margin should match within 5 degrees. If there is a significant discrepancy, investigate: incorrect component values, parasitic elements not in the model, layout issues (extra inductance in the feedback path), or measurement artifact (probe loading, injection transformer bandwidth).

description: Layout a power converter PCB for optimal electrical and thermal performance, covering power loop minimization, component placement strategy, copper pour design, thermal via arrays, and mixed-signal ground management.

steps.description: Identify all critical current loops in the converter topology and calculate the inductance requirement for each, establishing the layout priority hierarchy.

inputs.name: converter-schematic
inputs.desc: Complete schematic with all power stage components, gate drivers, and control circuitry

inputs.name: target-performance
inputs.desc: Maximum allowable voltage overshoot, EMI class target, and switching frequency that determine how critical loop inductance is

outputs.name: critical-loops-ranked
outputs.desc: Each current commutation loop identified and ranked by priority: hot loop (switching transition current), gate drive loop, bootstrap loop, output ripple loop, with target inductance for each

outputs.name: loop-inductance-budget
outputs.desc: Maximum allowable loop inductance for each critical loop, calculated from Vspike = L * di/dt with the acceptable overshoot and the switching di/dt

process: Identify the hot loop. This is the path through which current commutates during switching transitions. For a synchronous buck: high-side MOSFET drain -> input capacitor -> low-side MOSFET source -> low-side drain (= high-side source). During the dead time and switching transition, current changes at rates of 1-10 A/ns. Every nanohenry in this loop produces 1-10V of spike.

Calculate the inductance budget. For a 12V-to-1.2V buck at 20A with 400V/us switching and 2V allowable spike: L_max = 2V / (20A / 20ns) = 2nH. This is extremely tight and requires careful layout with the input capacitor immediately adjacent to the MOSFETs.

Identify the gate drive loop. From the driver IC output, through the gate resistor, to the MOSFET gate pin, return through the source pin to the driver ground, and through the driver bypass capacitor. Inductance here slows switching and causes gate ringing. Target: less than 5nH.

Identify the output loop. From the inductor output, through the output capacitor, to the load and return. This loop carries the AC ripple current at the switching frequency. Inductance here increases output ripple (Vnoise = L_loop * di/dt). Less critical than the hot loop but still important.

Rank the loops by priority: hot loop first (highest di/dt, highest overshoot impact), gate loop second (affects switching speed and EMI), output loop third. This ranking determines the component placement priority.

steps.description: Place power components to minimize critical loop areas, manage thermal paths, and separate noisy switching sections from sensitive analog and digital sections.

inputs.name: critical-loops-ranked
inputs.desc: Ranked current loops with target inductances

inputs.name: loop-inductance-budget
inputs.desc: Maximum inductance per loop

outputs.name: placement-plan
outputs.desc: Component placement on the PCB: power stage cluster with input caps immediately adjacent to MOSFETs, inductor placement, output cap bank, gate driver IC position, and control IC position with separation from switching node

outputs.name: keep-out-zones
outputs.desc: Keep-out zones under inductors (no sensitive traces), around switching nodes (high dv/dt), and clearance requirements for thermal management

process: Place the hot-loop components first. The high-side MOSFET, low-side MOSFET, and input decoupling capacitors form a tight cluster. Place the input caps between the MOSFET drain and source pads, on the same side of the board, as close as physically possible. For a half-bridge, the ideal layout has the two MOSFETs in a vertical stack with caps on either side.

Place the gate driver IC within 10mm of the MOSFET gates. The gate driver bypass capacitor goes directly across the driver Vcc and GND pins, on the same layer. Route the gate traces as short, wide paths. If using a bootstrap driver, the bootstrap cap and diode go between the driver and the high-side MOSFET.

Place the inductor. It connects from the switching node to the output. It is physically large and generates magnetic flux. Keep sensitive analog traces (feedback divider, current sense) away from the inductor magnetic field. Avoid routing any traces directly under the inductor unless they are on a ground plane layer.

Place the output capacitor bank at the inductor output, close to the load connection point. Multiple capacitors in parallel reduce ESR and ESL. Arrange them in a row with shared vias to the ground plane for minimal ESL contribution.

Place the control IC and analog components on the quiet side of the board, away from the switching node. The feedback voltage divider resistors should be close to the control IC, not close to the output capacitors (to avoid picking up switching noise through ground coupling). The current sense trace (if used) should be routed as a differential pair from the sense resistor to the control IC.

steps.description: Design the copper pours and thermal via arrays for current carrying capacity and heat spreading, balancing electrical performance with thermal management.

inputs.name: placement-plan
inputs.desc: Component placement with power flow paths identified

inputs.name: keep-out-zones
inputs.desc: Areas excluded from routing and pours

outputs.name: copper-pour-plan
outputs.desc: Copper pour allocation per layer: which layers carry power current, which are ground/reference planes, pour widths for current capacity (IPC-2152), and polygon connection strategy

outputs.name: thermal-via-specification
outputs.desc: Thermal via arrays under power components: via diameter, plating thickness, pitch, array size, and calculated thermal resistance contribution

process: Size copper traces and pours for current. IPC-2152 is the current standard for trace width vs current. For external layers with 1oz copper, 10A requires approximately 200mil (5mm) trace width for 20C rise in still air. Internal layers need wider traces (less heat dissipation). Use a calculator or the IPC charts for the exact width at your copper weight and temperature rise target.

Design the ground plane. A continuous, unbroken ground plane on one inner layer is ideal. It provides: low-impedance return path for all signals, reference plane for controlled impedance, electromagnetic shielding between layers. Do not split the ground plane unless absolutely required for mixed-signal isolation, and even then, connect the splits at a single point.

Thermal via arrays under power pads. For SMD power components (D2PAK, QFN exposed pad), thermal vias carry heat from the pad to inner copper layers and the bottom of the board. Via specification: 0.3mm drill diameter, 0.025mm copper plating (or filled and capped for better thermal conductivity). Pitch: 1.2mm center-to-center (standard drill), or 0.8mm for high-density. Each via contributes approximately 80 C/W thermal resistance. A 3x3 array of 9 vias: 80/9 = 9 C/W.

Via-in-pad considerations. For QFN and BGA packages, thermal vias directly in the pad provide the best thermal path. If using solder paste: use filled and capped vias to prevent solder wicking through the via (which creates voids under the pad). If blind vias are available: use blind microvias in the pad layer for zero wicking risk.

Power plane allocation for multi-layer boards. For a 4-layer board: Layer 1 = components and power routing, Layer 2 = ground plane (unbroken), Layer 3 = power planes (Vin, Vout), Layer 4 = components and routing. For a 6-layer board: add dedicated power layers for high-current paths. The switching node copper area should be minimized (it is a high dv/dt noise source) while maintaining adequate current capacity.

steps.description: Manage the ground system to prevent switching noise from corrupting sensitive analog measurements (voltage feedback, current sense, temperature) and digital control signals.

inputs.name: copper-pour-plan
inputs.desc: Copper and ground plane allocation

inputs.name: thermal-via-specification
inputs.desc: Via placement that may affect ground plane integrity

outputs.name: ground-strategy
outputs.desc: Ground connection scheme: single ground plane with strategic routing to keep high-current return paths away from sensitive signals, or star ground point if plane is not feasible

outputs.name: sensitive-trace-routing
outputs.desc: Routing rules for feedback divider, current sense, reference voltage, and communication signals (I2C, SPI, UART): trace placement, guard traces, and via-free zones

process: Understand ground current flow. In a buck converter, the high-frequency switching current flows in the hot loop: Vin cap -> high-side MOSFET -> switching node -> low-side MOSFET -> ground -> back to Vin cap. This return current flows through the ground plane under the hot loop. Any sensitive circuitry in this return path picks up noise via the shared impedance.

Route the hot loop return current away from the control IC. The power ground (high-current return) and signal ground (control IC reference, feedback divider return) should connect to the ground plane at separate points, with the signal ground connection on the quiet side of the board. This is a star ground implemented on a plane.

Feedback voltage divider routing. The divider resistors connect from Vout to the control IC feedback pin to ground. Route the trace from the divider output to the FB pin as a short, direct path close to the ground plane. Do not route it near the switching node or inductor. Place a small filter cap (100pF-1nF) at the FB pin to ground to reject high-frequency noise.

Current sense routing. If using a sense resistor in the power path: route the sense traces as a differential pair, directly from the resistor kelvin pads, away from the switching node, to the current sense input of the controller. Guard traces on both sides tied to ground can reject capacitively coupled noise.

Communication and digital signal routing. I2C/SPI/UART to the BMS or controller: route these on the quiet side of the board, away from switching power. Add series termination resistors (22-100 ohms) at the source to reduce ringing. For long runs (more than 50mm), add ground guard traces. Keep digital signals away from the analog feedback path to prevent clock noise coupling into the regulation loop.

steps.description: Review the complete power PCB layout for manufacturing feasibility, IPC compliance, and perform a final checklist covering all critical design rules before releasing to fabrication.

inputs.name: ground-strategy
inputs.desc: Ground management plan

inputs.name: sensitive-trace-routing
inputs.desc: Sensitive signal routing completed

outputs.name: design-review-checklist
outputs.desc: Completed checklist covering: hot loop area verification, gate loop area, thermal path continuity, clearance and creepage, solder paste apertures for power components, and test point accessibility

outputs.name: manufacturing-notes
outputs.desc: Fabrication and assembly notes: copper weight, via fill specification, impedance-controlled layers, special paste or stencil requirements for fine-pitch or thermal pads, and inspection criteria

process: Verify critical loop areas. Measure the hot loop area using the 3D stackup: trace length * layer-to-layer separation. For a 4-layer board with 0.2mm dielectric: a 20mm hot loop trace on layer 1 returning on layer 2 has area = 20mm * 0.2mm = 4mm^2. This produces ~5nH. If the budget is 2nH, the trace must be shorter or the return path must be on the same layer.

Verify clearance and creepage. IPC-2221 and IEC 62368: for 400V working voltage, minimum clearance = 2.5mm (sea level), creepage = 6.4mm (Pollution Degree 2, Material Group III). These apply between input and output if isolation is required, and between any conductor and exposed metal. Slots in the PCB can reduce creepage requirements by creating air gaps.

Verify thermal paths. Every power component must have a defined thermal path to ambient: through the PCB (thermal vias to a copper pour or heat sink), through the package top (heat sink attached), or through airflow (forced air over an exposed pad). Use the calculated thermal resistance to verify no component exceeds its temperature limit.

Solder paste and stencil review. For large thermal pads (QFN, D2PAK): reduce the stencil aperture to 50-80% coverage using a window pattern (multiple small rectangles instead of one large one) to prevent solder voids and tombstoning. For fine-pitch ICs (0.5mm pitch): reduce aperture width to 80% of pad width. Step-down stencil areas if there are mixed large and small components.

Test point accessibility. Add test points for: input voltage, output voltage, switching node (for scope probe access), gate drive signals, current sense, key control IC pins (feedback, compensation, soft-start). Place switching node test points as short stubs to minimize probe-induced ringing. Add a dedicated ground test point (a large, easily accessible pad) for the scope probe ground spring.

description: Achieve timing closure in FPGA designs through constraint-driven synthesis, clock domain analysis, setup and hold time verification, pipelining strategies, and systematic debugging of timing failures.

steps.description: Define and analyze the clock architecture: all clock domains, their relationships (synchronous, asynchronous, phase-shifted), clock generation resources (PLLs, buffers), and jitter budgets.

inputs.name: design-specification
inputs.desc: Top-level block diagram with all clock domains, their frequencies, and the interfaces between domains

inputs.name: fpga-target
inputs.desc: Target FPGA device family and speed grade, with its PLL specifications, clock routing resources, and timing model

outputs.name: clock-tree-specification
outputs.desc: Complete clock tree: PLL configuration (input frequency, output frequencies, feedback mode), global vs regional clock buffer assignment, clock enable usage for gated clocks

outputs.name: clock-domain-crossing-map
outputs.desc: Matrix of all clock domain crossings in the design, classified as: same-source synchronous (safe with constraints), asynchronous (requires synchronizer), or rate-related (requires FIFO or handshake)

process: List every clock in the design. For each: source (pin, PLL output, divided from another clock), frequency, duty cycle, and jitter. Group clocks by source: clocks from the same PLL output or derived by integer division are synchronous. Clocks from different sources (different PLLs, different input pins) are asynchronous.

Map the PLL configuration. Use the FPGA vendor's PLL wizard to configure each PLL: input reference clock, VCO frequency (must fall within the PLL VCO range), output dividers for each clock domain. Minimize the number of PLLs (each PLL has lock time and consumes resources). Lock signal: use it to hold the design in reset until PLLs are locked.

Identify all clock domain crossings. For each crossing: single-bit signals need a 2-register synchronizer. Multi-bit buses need either a FIFO (for streaming data), a handshake protocol (for control/status), or gray-code encoding (for counters). Document each crossing with its type, data width, and throughput requirement.

Jitter budget. The total jitter from input pin through PLL to the flip-flop clock input must leave enough margin for setup and hold times. Tclk_period - Tsetup - Thold - Tjitter_total = timing margin. If jitter consumes too much margin, reduce clock frequency or use a cleaner reference clock.

Clock enable vs multiple clocks. Using clock enables (CE) instead of separate slow clocks keeps everything on the same clock domain and avoids CDC issues. A 100MHz clock with a CE that pulses every 4th cycle behaves like a 25MHz clock but with no domain crossing. Use this wherever possible to simplify the design.

steps.description: Write timing constraints (SDC format) that fully describe the design intent: clock definitions, input/output delays, false paths, multicycle paths, and clock group relationships.

inputs.name: clock-tree-specification
inputs.desc: Clock architecture with all clock sources and domains

inputs.name: clock-domain-crossing-map
inputs.desc: All CDC points and their synchronization methods

outputs.name: timing-constraints-file
outputs.desc: Complete SDC file with: create_clock for all clocks, create_generated_clock for derived clocks, set_input_delay and set_output_delay for all I/O, set_false_path for asynchronous CDC, set_multicycle_path where applicable

outputs.name: constraint-coverage-report
outputs.desc: Percentage of paths constrained: unconstrained paths are potential bugs. Target 100% constraint coverage with explicit false paths or multicycle paths for all exceptions

process: Define primary clocks. create_clock for every clock input pin, with the exact period and waveform. For a 100MHz clock: create_clock -period 10.0 -waveform {0 5.0} [get_ports clk_100m]. Use the actual period, not a rounded value.

Define generated clocks. For PLL outputs: create_generated_clock -source [get_pins pll/clkin] -multiply_by 2 [get_pins pll/clkout_200m]. For divided clocks in logic: create_generated_clock -source [get_pins clk_reg/Q] -divide_by 4 [get_pins clk_div4_reg/Q]. The tool must know the relationship between clocks to analyze inter-domain paths.

Set I/O delays. For every input pin: set_input_delay -clock <source_clock> -max <Tco_max + Tpd_max> [get_ports data_in]. For outputs: set_output_delay -clock <dest_clock> -max <Tsetup_dest> [get_ports data_out]. These tell the tool what timing the outside world expects. Unconstrained I/O is a common source of timing failures in the lab.

Set false paths for asynchronous CDCs. Signals crossing between unrelated clock domains through proper synchronizers: set_false_path -from [get_clocks clk_a] -to [get_clocks clk_b]. This removes these paths from timing analysis (they are handled by the synchronizer design, not by meeting setup time). Only set false paths where a synchronizer is actually present.

Set multicycle paths. For paths that have multiple clock cycles to settle (e.g., a result that is valid every 2 cycles): set_multicycle_path -setup 2 -from [get_pins src_reg/Q] -to [get_pins dst_reg/D]. This relaxes the setup requirement by one cycle. Also set the hold multicycle: set_multicycle_path -hold 1 -from ... -to ... to maintain the correct hold check edge.

steps.description: Run synthesis and place-and-route, analyze the timing report, and identify the root causes of timing failures for systematic resolution.

inputs.name: timing-constraints-file
inputs.desc: SDC constraints applied to the design

inputs.name: constraint-coverage-report
inputs.desc: Verification that all paths are constrained

outputs.name: timing-report-analysis
outputs.desc: Categorized timing failures: setup violations (logic depth, fanout, routing congestion) and hold violations (short paths, clock skew), with the critical path for each failing endpoint

outputs.name: root-cause-classification
outputs.desc: Each failure classified: excessive logic levels (needs pipelining), high fanout (needs replication), long routing (needs floorplanning), clock skew (needs constraint adjustment), or constraint error (needs SDC fix)

process: Run synthesis with timing-driven optimization. Enable retiming (register balancing) if the tool supports it. Set the effort level to high for the initial analysis. Review the synthesis log for warnings: inferred latches (almost always a bug), unconstrained paths, and clock domain issues.

Run place-and-route. Use timing-driven placement. After placement, run an initial timing analysis. If timing is met after placement, route with timing optimization. If timing fails after placement, debug before routing (routing cannot improve a bad placement).

Read the timing report. For each failing path: note the slack (negative = failing), the data path delay (logic + routing), the clock path delay (launch to capture), and the setup/hold requirement. The path detail shows each element: flip-flop Tco, LUT delay, routing delay, and flip-flop Tsetup.

Classify failures. Logic-depth limited: if the data path has more than 6-8 logic levels, the delay through LUTs exceeds the clock period. Fix: pipeline (insert registers). High-fanout limited: if a signal drives hundreds of flip-flops, the routing delay to reach them all is large. Fix: register replication (the tool can do this automatically with the right directive). Routing-congested: if the routing delay is 2-3x the logic delay, the placer put connected elements too far apart. Fix: floorplanning constraints or reducing utilization.

Check hold violations separately. Hold violations are usually fixed by the tool automatically (by adding delay buffers). If they persist, it typically indicates a clock skew issue or a false path that should have been constrained. Hold violations are dangerous because they cause functional failures that are not frequency-dependent.

steps.description: Apply pipelining, retiming, and logic optimization techniques to close timing on failing paths, trading latency for throughput where necessary.

inputs.name: timing-report-analysis
inputs.desc: Failing paths identified with delay breakdown

inputs.name: root-cause-classification
inputs.desc: Failure causes classified for targeted fixes

outputs.name: rtl-modifications
outputs.desc: Specific RTL changes: pipeline registers inserted at optimal points (cutting the longest combinational path), logic restructured to reduce depth, and fanout-limited signals identified for replication

outputs.name: timing-improvement-verification
outputs.desc: Timing results after each modification, showing the slack improvement on the targeted paths and verifying no new failures were introduced

process: Pipeline insertion. Identify the longest combinational path and insert a register at the midpoint. This halves the path delay at the cost of one cycle of latency. For a pipeline with balanced stages: Fmax_pipelined = 1 / max(Tstage_i). The goal is to make all stages roughly equal in delay.

Retiming. The synthesis tool can move registers forward or backward through combinational logic without changing the functionality (if the initial state is handled). Enable retiming: the tool automatically rebalances register placement to equalize path delays. This is especially effective for datapath-heavy designs (DSP, filter chains).

Logic restructuring. A long chain of additions (a + b + c + d) creates a linear dependency. Restructure as a tree: (a+b) + (c+d) reduces the depth from 3 to 2. Similarly, priority encoders can be restructured as balanced trees. Conditional assignments (if-elsif-elsif chain) create priority logic; if the conditions are mutually exclusive, use a case statement for parallel evaluation.

Fanout reduction. For a reset signal that fans out to every register in the design: use a pipeline of reset registers, one per major functional block, each driving a local fanout tree. Alternatively, set max_fanout synthesis directives and let the tool replicate registers.

Iterate. After each RTL change: re-synthesize, re-place, re-route, and re-analyze timing. Verify that the targeted path improved and that no new paths failed. The optimization converges when all paths meet timing with positive slack. Record the final Fmax and the worst-case slack.

steps.description: Verify all clock domain crossings are properly synchronized, run a structural CDC check, and sign off the design for timing closure with documentation.

inputs.name: rtl-modifications
inputs.desc: Finalized RTL with all timing fixes

inputs.name: timing-improvement-verification
inputs.desc: Timing reports showing all paths pass

outputs.name: cdc-verification-report
outputs.desc: Structural CDC analysis results: all crossings identified, synchronizer structure verified (2-register minimum, no combinational logic between stages), and any unsynchronized crossings flagged as bugs

outputs.name: timing-signoff-package
outputs.desc: Complete timing closure documentation: SDC file, timing summary at worst-case PVT corner (slow process, low voltage, high temperature), CDC report, and list of any timing waivers with justification

process: Run a structural CDC analysis. Tools (Synopsys SpyGlass, Cadence Conformal, or open-source ClocknWork) parse the RTL and identify every signal that crosses between clock domains. For each crossing, verify: a 2-stage synchronizer exists (two back-to-back flip-flops on the destination clock), no combinational logic between the synchronizer stages, and multi-bit buses use FIFO or handshake (not just synchronizers on each bit).

Check for common CDC bugs. Reconvergence: if two synchronized versions of the same signal reconverge in combinational logic, they can glitch because the synchronizers may resolve metastability at different times. Gray coding for counters: only one bit changes per transition, so a single synchronizer per bit is safe. Binary counters across domains need a FIFO.

Verify timing at worst-case PVT (Process, Voltage, Temperature) corner. For setup: slow process, low voltage (Vmin), high temperature (125C). For hold: fast process, high voltage (Vmax), low temperature (-40C or 0C). The final timing report must show positive slack at both corners for all constrained paths.

Generate the signoff package. Include: the final SDC constraint file with comments explaining each exception (false path, multicycle), the timing summary report at worst-case corners, the CDC report with all crossings classified and verified, and any timing waivers (paths that fail timing with explanation of why it is acceptable, e.g., a test-only path).

Final verification. Run a gate-level simulation with timing annotation (SDF back-annotation) to verify functional correctness at the actual delays. This catches timing issues that static analysis may miss, such as glitches on asynchronous resets or metastability effects. Run at worst-case and best-case corners.
